Ilome-bound—The bed-eidden patient. Fun, like ice-cream, is beat enjoyed at somebody elso's expense. - -; Young physicians should not-be discouraged because they find it difficult to get ufto practice. All that they need for success is plenty of 'patients. A little girl ate her dinner with so good an appetite, that by the lime dessert Was placed on the table she ,could eat no more. She vit silent and sorrtwful, and looked mournfully at the dainties which !IT piled on her plate. "Why don't you eat, my darling ?" asked her fond and anxious 'mother. "Oh, mamma!" cried the disconsolate infaut, "because onlyLtey eyes are hungry."

, How to LIVE ON Fr URlsteiCli A DAY.—About a quarter -of a century ago, in the pretty, town of Accringthn, a movement was set on foot by the proprietors of a large printworks to persuade the townspeople, especially the employes of the werks, to adopt the vegetarian system O f living; and in order to further the movement a tea party was arranged to be held at the works, and several ,eminent vegetarians were invited to make speeches on the subject. For the tea a charge of Bd. each person -was made. and-the attendance was large. Tea over and 'tables cleared, the respected head of the firm was voted to the chair, and commenced the real business of the ,evening by a-vigorous speech on vegetarianism. Other speeches followed, and nearly all present seemed satisfied that the doctrines expounded only required to be put into prattice by the people for them to reap the benefit of better health and cheaper modes of living. There was, however, an old woman present who, after listening intently, rose and said—"Mester Cheermon, if yo pleas, sur, might lax yo a question?" "Of course you can, my good woman," was the kindly reply of the:chair- man. "Wee!, sur, I have listened very weel tO what yo and those gents fro' London av said about this, that, and Collier, to eat and live upon fourpence a day, but I can- not understand how it is as yo charged us eightpence for our tay !"-IVt-Bits. SECRET FAULTS.—It is past denial that we all have ffaults of which others know nothing. In some respects we know ourselves better than we are known to our most intimate companions; for they see but the outside, while we know all that goes an within. Each dm lives s hidden life—a secret, inner life; we live a life which -sometimes shows itself in our conduct, and so reveals it- self to onlookers, but which is often in strange contra- diction to outward shows. We cannot thoroughly know a man by observing hi behaviour, any more than we can be sure of the contents of a house by looking at it from without, or of a new book by reading the title on the cover. The real man is behind all appearances, and may quite falsify- them. A• calm face may mask a troubled mind. A mean and sordid nature may co-exist with a great display of charity. We all live behind 'a veil. We have a friend, perhaps, with whom we aeo accustomed to share our deepest thoughts, and who knows us better than any other; but even he does met know everything; he never will.•S`aone secret chamber ' we keep locked; we give the key to no one. This applies to our faults. Men know that we are imperfect, bat they do not know hew imperfect we are. We all airily with us the remembrance of sins—sins of thought and I deed, of irpagination and desire, which have never been known to any mortal but ourselves. It is one of the penalties attaching to the wondrous and blessed power of memory that we cannot forget the faults of the past, however much we may wish to forget them. In real life there is no Lethe, even for the sins of which we most bitterly repent. Many a gpod man, as he thinkeef his secret faults, feels that any'repute he may have forgood- ness is almost fraudulent; he is distressed rather than gratified by it. Did men know him as he knows himself (he thinks), how different would their judgment be!— " The Quiver," far:Mare& LAUGHING LANCASHlRE.—Lancashire laughs when its mills are full and its mill-hands busy—when the wheels of the cotton-gods grind quickly. The Lancashire opera- tive takes life then more easily than his master; his wages are regular, his cares are fewer, and his heart is lighter. He can snap his fingers at the Fates. He works hard and well, but he has his leisure after work, and a few pence will whirl him from the factories to the sea when he is disposed for a change of air from Saturday to Monday, and where the stiff breeze from over the Irish Sea will meet him in his character of a "Tail of the Weeker" on the low-lying sandy coast, and will do hitn as much good—probably more—than the master who is talalaa his month "right off the reel." Lancashire was Crots at the time our story opens. Liverpool and .:Chester, Preston and Wigan, Blackburn and Bolton, Oldham and Bury, were all reputed to be doing well and -waxing fat, despite the minimum of grumblers who had of course, and as usual, never known such times rßst Lancashire was really flourishing—the mills and mines bad more than their full complement of hands, there was less misery in the courts and alleys of the big black towns, where misery always lurks; less sickness, and less crime. There was more talk of pleasant holidays, of wakes and general junketting3 there was more money spent right and left throughout the land, and Lancashire can spend its cash freely when it chooses, and hold its own with any county—aye, and give long odds. _There were rare doings that summer at the .great pleasure resort of Scarletpool in Lancashire—there was no end of business, and no end to the streains:of people ebbing and flowing in their thousands between the two great railway stations and the sea. A southerner accus- t°rsed th the mild distractions of his Eastbourne and his Hastings to the fashionable frivolities of Brighton, and the peace and quietness of Seaford, would have stood amazed—and horror-stricken, perhaps—at the force and vigour and boisterous life and hearty amuse- ments and thorough enjoyment and "go" of this bustling and noisy Scarletpool that year, thronged from end to end of its three-and-a-half miles of parade, by legions of good-tempered handicraftsmen, with their wives and children, their country cousins and sweethearts, and ll the friends, relations, and acquaintances they had mus- tered together for an outing—for an escape from the towns lying in their smoke and smother in the heart ')f a busy land, and missing not their stray childrol amongst the few millions left behind to work, and wait their turn to play.—Nee Story in Cassell's Saturday Jaufrned. LOUIS NAPOLEON AND Ms CAPTORS.—Here is a Pleas- ing incident in the career of Napoleon lll.S.which took place while he was with the camp at Boulogne in 11854 : —" On arriving at Boulogne, the Emperor commissioned M. Ducos,the Minister of the Marine, to find:out if there still existed in that town any of the men who were con- cerned in his arrest on the occasion of his ill-fated expe- dition in 1840. Duces discovered a sailor who had thrown himself into the sea to seize the Prince, who was trying to swim back to the vessel in which he had come, the aforesaid sailor having clutched the Pretender by his hair; then Ducos, also discovered a gendarme, elan a Custom House officer, who, on the beach, had received he vanquished Prince from the hands of the sailor and had taken him by the collar. These two men were brought to Duce, who asked them if they were really the persons that had been designated to him? The two poor devils replied, with much hesitation, that it was they who had arrested the Prince, and Duces ordered them to return the next morning- at 9 30. After an anxious night they presented themselves before the Minister exactly at the appointed hour. Duces con- ducted them before the Emperor, and the sailor was the one first admitted to the Imperial presence. The Em- peror, twisting his long moustache, walked quickly up to him, and said, 'So it was von that in 1840 sprang into the sea and captured use by seizing me by the hair?' The sailor, 'Your Majesty, s--s The Emperor, Look here; was it you? Yes or eioa The sailor (re- covering his self-possession), Well, yes, Your majesty all the others were firing at you and you might have been wounded and got drowned ; so I Jumped into the sea to save your life—it was I who 'saved Your life? The Emperor and the Minister had hard work to keepitheir faces straight while listening to this emtellished history of an arrest changed tea rescue. Well done, my good fellow,' replied the Emperor, 'here is the cross that you have won in doing your duty, and here is 500 francs as a souvenir from me.' Next came the gendarme Custom House officer, but hi imagination was less inventive than that of the sailor, and suggested to him no such marvellous transactions. He stammered and hesitated some time, then, bravely making up his mind, he re- 'Yes, sire, it was I. You were breaking the laws. I was on duty, and I arrested you.' The Emperor, 'And that cross that your wear—who gave it to you?' The gendarme, 'Sire., it was King Louis Philippe.' The Em- peror, For having arrested me?' The gendarme, 'lnns - an old soldier—l have done good service,--I but tell the truth, sire, it was on the occasion of your arrest I re- ceived it.' The Emperor, • I am parry for it, because I shall not have the pleasure of giving it to pelf myself tencdeaiyou have already got it; but here is the military (taking off the one that he wore himself and fastening it to the breast of the gendarme's uniforin). You are a brave soldier." And the gendarme received, as as the sailor had already done, a gift of 500 francs.' What we CO on. Tic • ..pmarks in life mute, con= pe things ME fry. .in the light of memory! is glove which is the result of admiratAn and resion,and this will often cling to its imperfect object' to tha end. - ' _ '•' Some women know what is told them if told plainly; others look into the eyes of those around them and see what is sought to be concealed. , , Emetion, if *forced, lute little poWer except to repel, but 1 even a glimpse of a deep, suppressed feeling haunts the memory, especially if its cause is half in mystery. It scarcely seems possible for one to become a sympa- thetic musician without a large degree of imagination and a nature easily moved by thought aad feeling. No cosnedian can make as laughable a face as that made by the dmall boy when he brings a jelly jar down from the closet shei and discovers it to be full of tea- penny nails. - Man and poets are always imagining that women ease mysteries. The lea is, they are as transparent as glass when they knoVr their own minds; when they don't who else should knew them ? All contact leaves its Mark. We are taking into our- selves the werld about us, the society in which we move, the impress of every sympathetic contact with good or evil, and we she'll carry titers with us for ever. We do not pass through a world for naught; it folkcws us be- cause it has become part ef us. , f The preperty-master of a theatre is usually very ingeni- ous, very industrious, and not toe highly p told. When a live elephant was once brought upon the stage In a piece in Drury Lane Theatre, the property-master left the house in disgust. "If I couldn't make a better elephant than that," be said, "I should be jolly well ashamed of myself!" EVery human soul has the germ of some flowers within; and they would open if they could only find sunshine and free air to expand in. I always told you that not having enough sunshine WaS what ailed the world. Make the people happy, and there will not be half the quarreling or a tenth part of the wickedness 'there is.—Lydia Maria Child. Twarrartm-russ.—Said a very old man, "Some folks are always complaining about the weather, but I am very thankful when I wake up in the m,orning and find any weather at all." We may smile at the simplicity of the old man, but still his language indicates a spirit that contributes much to calm and peaceful life. It is bettor and wiser to cultivate that spirit than to be always com- plaining of things as we are. Be thankful for such mer- cies as you have, and if God sees it will be for youngood and His glory He will give you many more. At least, do not make yourself and others unhappy by your ingrati- tude and complaints. A Motrrwrim OF BREAD.—A new and successfudmhari- table work in-Paris is called "L'eeuvre de la bowl& de pain" (the .work of a mouthful of bread). It is thus described :-" It is a sort of shed, furnished simply with two long benches and a kind of counter. Anyone who likes may go in, and, on taking a seat, is immediately waited upon by a tidily-clad woman, who pasties round a basket containing slices of bread. His slice of bread finished, the new comer goes to the counter, where he its handed a glass of water flavoured with a few drops or vinegar, which,-having drunk, he goes his way without question being asked as to whe he is, whence he , comes, or whither he goes. It would be easy to estab- lish similar systems of relief in the poorer districts of other cities. None but the really destitute-would be ' tempted,bysuch fare, and a slice of bread and a cup of cold water thus promptly supplied might often save ..a, some poor helpless one from despair." WHICH WAS THE BEAVER ?—I Will tell yon about two boys who were at school at Eton, and who were both very brave, though they did not either figlit an enemy, or seize a mad dog, This is what they did—They both went out iliooting one day, and were seenty a master. One boy managed to run away and hide in a ditch till all danger was past, but the other was caught and flogged severely. And not only did this happen, but the latter was told that unless he would give the name of the laoy who was with him, he should be flogged again until he did. The boy refused, and bore the punishment rather than the other should have to stiffer; but pre- sently his companion rushed into the room with his, throat bandaged up, and confessed that he had shooting too. As he was ill in bed with a sore tiLl aeet brought on-by biding in the ditch, the masters forgave: them both. I think you will agree with me that it re- quired a great deal of moral courage to make a bay get 1 out of bed, and run the chance of a flogging, to save his 1 friend from suffering any more; and it is hard to say ' which was the braver of the two.—" Little Folks" Maga- zine for Maroh. - : . ' A Tsui ow Tarts.—There is at present up North a sportsman, well known as a first-rate rider to hounds and a skilful 'cross-country jockey, who may be referred to, says ,a contemporary, as Gay Tiepleton. Amongst Gay's little weaknesses is a propensity to practic IL joking. At a country- house not long ago, when the ladies had retird for the evening, the gentlemen congregated in the smat.ing-room to discuss politics and other abstruse liquids. Enter one of the guests, whom we will call young Ewart. Gay Tippleton glanced at him, and observed, "I say, Ewart, I think it's very bad form of you coming in here wi:hout taking the trouble to go up stairs and change your coat. You'll go inte the drawing-room to-morrow amongst the ladies with an atmosphere of tobacco all about you. I've a good mlild 1 to out the tails off yottr coat and melte &smoking-jacket 0 , It! If you do it again, I shall certainly have those tails off." "Oh, I couldn't be bothered to go up stairs!" Ewan said. "I'm only going to have a 'cigarette, and off to bed, for I'm tired." Next evening—scene repeated—young Ewart strolls into the smoking-room with his dress-coat on. To him Gay Templeton: "Hallos, Ewan, you're at It again I gave you dce warning, and yoa loso.wa I always keep my word. I must have your tails.' And, with little more ale, Gay and a few congenial spirits had young Ewart dowa on a conch, and cut the tails off his coat. Ewart took It very coolly. He strolled up to the fire, and stood in the attitude ladies allege to be the favourite one of the male sex, only he had no trouble in holding up his tails. "You take it very philosoOically," said one of Gay Tippleton's friends. "Oh," replied Ewan, "it dsesn't matter to me ! lea not my coat; it's T;ppleton'e garment. I knew he'd keep his word; so I just dropped into his room in passing and put his coat on." There was a roar of laughter, and, to do Gay Tippleton justice, no one joined in it more heartily than he. Ten BUGLE-CALLS OF THE ENGLISH Antam—Consider- ing the length of some of the calls, it may surprise the reader to Ipar that there are only five different notes played on the bugle, and, though that is the case, the language of the instrument is not at all limited. A lan- guage with only five words might be thought easy to learn, and yet the different arrangements of these.' " words " ("sentences," as I may call them) are endleisf It is, indeed, a very nesessary part of a soldier's training. to learn the language of the bugle, and even unmusical men soon acquire it,. For, in the first place, the same- " calls" sound much about the same time each day—a hungry recruit, for instance, does not take long to recog- nise the "Dinner Bugle," nor does the careless soldier' forget the summons to extra drill, much as he might wish to de So. The men in their barrack-roomsr,too often associate words with the notes of the bugle, and that is a help to remember the meaning of the sounds heard. I will first explain as to the instrument itself, that the notes are all made with the lip and tongue ; there are no keys used, as is the case with most brass instruments; they are all notes of the common chord; and, although bugles are always in the key of B flat, music for them is written in the key of C. It will be easily understood that no great knowledge of the prin- ciples of music is necessary to play an matruntent So limited in its capacity; a correct ear, a thorough acquain- tance with time—for even dotted semiquavers occur fre- quently,—and a power of learning by heart all the dif- ferent calls: inn the chief essentials. The authorised course of insirtiction for a bugler is to begin by playing the lowest note with all the variations of time of dune- tion. The same exercises are then taught on the second note, G; these two notes are then combined in a variety of ways, after which the original one note exercises are taken on the third note of the bugle; and when perfect in that note exercises are played with the three notes combined, and so on with the others.—Cassell's Family Magazine. ' Toe WILDEST OF LtnENDs.—Of the Hindoo le,„vends the most striking feature is their wildness. Lal Behari's tales are wilder than the wildest bits of the Arabian Nights." A young man puts an egg of the toontoOnia bird into a cupboard, and out of it comes a bird that grows into the loveliest girl the world ever saw. The mannik stone in some snakes' heads is worth the wealth

of seven kings. In a certain city an elephant is king- maker; but the king of his choice only reigns a day, for out of the queen's mouth comes a thread-like snake, which slays him in the bridal chamber. A long-lost siin who had fallen in love with his mother, and has mounted the cow-house roof that he may break .in and carry her off, happily hears his life's story from two calves that are quietly discussing him below. Ghosts haunt 'pee- pul trees, and are as tricky as mediums at a seance. A wife going out of doors on. a dark night accidentally knocksup against a Sankchinni, white lady ghost, that sat on a low branch. The revengeful creature at once took her by the throat, thrust her into a hole in:the tree, and went in, taking her shape so completell that the mother-in-law, that universal inmate of the Hindu hut, was deceived. The only difference was that whereas the wife had been weak and languid the ghost was brisk and active, "She has turned over a new leaf; so much the better," said the mother-in-law, when the errands and the cooking were done in next to no time. But one day the old woman caught sight of the ghost fetching some- thing from the next room ghost-fashion, by streyching out a long arm--for ghosts can stretch their limbs a great way—though not as far as Rakshasis can. She said nothing, but told her son and they watched, and before long they saw the kitchen hearth ablaze, though they knew there 'was no fire in the house. Looking through a chink they saw that the wife had thrust her foot into the oven, and that it was burning like a bit of wood. "She's a ghost," they whispered, as they went for the ojha, who testified her by burning turmeric under her nose. She proved her ghostship by scream- ing, and was then beaten with slippers till she confessed and showed where the real wife was, and was again beaten until she promised never to do the family any further harm. The poor wife must have been a bad bargain after the active ghost, for she was almost dead, and very slowly got back to her usual weak health. There is more diffetence between. creams than between the best specittiens of churns. 1 Two valuable lots of Herefords were shipped' for Amoriea last week, ono lot of about SO heifers shipped by Mr. George Leigh, of Aurora, Kane County, lairtois, for the firm of wkich he is the head; the other let, also about 30 heifers, shipped by Mr. W. E. Britten, of Pres- Iteigra for Mr. Adams Earl, of La Fayette, Indiara. Cows ma TEE DATllT.—Speaking at the Contention of New York State Dairymen, Major Alford said he believed the best cross for dairy cows was that between Jersey , and Ayrshire, the Jersey to be the sire and the Ayrshire the dam; that was if they wanted to cross two Tam breeds. The quality came from the sire, the quantity and other characteristics from the dam. He had not an animal ill his herd that did not give him 3001b5. of butter a year, but he was not satisfied with that for a standard. He believed that the best dairy Cows were grade animals. Ho was in a Canada dairy of 20 cows last summer, 10 of which had given 5001 ha ef butter each in a7year. KERING PORK.—A very successful raiser of pork says that one great point in his management was to com- mence the growing and fattening process as soon as the young pigs began to eat other food than the new milk • they commenced with. Pigs which he wanted were kept Igrowing all the time. They had clean, dry, warm, and comfortable quarters, and a regular supply of food. As a proof of the excellence of his management, six pigs, in one instance, eight •months and seven days old, gave ' a dressed weight of 2,031 lbs., the heaviest weighing 398 , lbs. His heaviest animal was fattened from a pig ' which, early in April, weighed 214 lbs., and in the first Iweek in November following, the dressed weight was 788 lbs. IThe DEVELOP/Mil OF Smelt HORSES.—The celebrated , horse, England's Glory (705), was foaled in 1814, and is ' one of the early sires that figure in the Cart Horse Stud Book. The Shirea have plenty of modern history con- / nected with their doings, and we have no difficulty in perceiving an astonishing rate of progress going on yearly in their style and conformation, that alas secured for them a high degree of favour and popularity. But the history of the Shires, or the old stage-waggon horse, is very meagre, and barely furnishes any information Iprevious to the middlaof the last century. It is matter of regret to very many ag,ticulturists that ancient writers were-so reticent on the various breeds of live stock, that were kept by the yeomen of this country in past ages. Tim Mize Taarie.—A writer in the Dairy Farmer , says :—Now farnaers are all rushing into the new milk I business, 'the maramt is altogether overdone. Milk, at I the stations can hardly be given away, and the dealers ' are cutting prices lower and lower; in fact, prices are far below cost of production. It is hard to say what is to be done to Ray our rent, ac., now we have taken the advice given with the best intention, viz., to go in for dairying, which would be our salvation, has turned out wrong, and having invested our little remaining capital in cows, and finding that also a losing game, we cannot now sell out our cows, for everyone finding the game s , losing one, is anxious to get out of their cows, and they ' can only be sold at a loss, and our capital is still further Idepleted. Some landlords say we do not try to help , ourselves. I wonder how they would succeed on the same terms. Mn. JESSE COLLINGS' PEASANT PROPRIETARY SILL." The Warwickshire Chamber of Agriculture discussed this bill on Saturday, at a special meeting held at the Shire Hall,•"Wartvick.. The Chairman stigmatised the bill as more suited for. the French Commune than the British Parliatneni, and. Mr. Trepplin, a tenant farmer, said it was Communistic and Utopian, and a catch-vote measure. Mr. -Ramsden submitted a proposition 'con- demning the bill as impractical and prejudicial to all parties. He adduced figures to show that land which , could now be rented at 30s. would cost the peasant pro- prietor.= 15,5. If the farmer could not make it pay at 'the former, price how could the peasant proprietor at • the latter, without capital or modern appliances? He also objected to the entire principle of the bill, which would allow the best parts of farms to he seized by any- one. Major Fosbery seconded the motion, and said during the present century two or three royal commis- sions had shown peasant proprietorships to be a failure. The bill would be disastrous to anyone who came under it. A labourer with no capital could not stand a single adverse season or avail himself of improved modern ap- pliances. To attempt to elevate labourers into peasant proprietors at a step was contrary to the principles of political economy. Mr. Palmer and Mr. Lloyd supported the resolution, which was then unanimously adopted. M/LIC Fa:vela—Question: I have read various opinions in agricultural and other papers as to what hi- the- cause of milk fever or dropping after calving. As it is a cora- plaint which occurs among valuable animals, and is seen in amore or less severe form all over England, I should like to know your veterinary correspondent's ideas on this important subject. —Answer : Milk fever or dropping -after calving (tecnically knowmas parturient apoplexy) is a disease which has received a great ainount of atten- tion by veterinarians of late, anti justly'so, fori consider it one of the ~most serious -diseases of the tow with which we have to deal. There is; however, a great diversity of opinions as to the actual cause of this se- rious and frequently fatal complaint, and from time to time numerous theories on this subject have been ad- vanced, but after giving each due consideration I cannot end one that, to my mind, satisfactorily explains the symptoms of this disease, and the reason why it occurs only under certain conditions. I will mention a few of the principal theories advanced and, then in as plain language as passible state what my own !particular views are with regard to the causes of true milk fever or parturient apoplexy, but before doing so I must in- form my readers that there are other diseases of a totally different nature which are often confounded with it, the chief of these being inflammation of the womb, paraly- -8139 injuries to the hindquarters at the time of calving, &C. FARMERS' DEBATING Socrarres.—We are not going to be so rash as to suppose that the formation of farmers' debating societiesowould be a panacea for all our ills; but we venture to express the belief that they would be very helpful in more ways than one. We regret the re- ticence and reluctance on the part of farmers to meet together for the purpose of debating matters even of the greatest moment in connection with their, own affairs; but doubtless the defect might be overcome. There is no other class of society so;grievously behind the times in this respect as the farmers. It is most de- sirable that we should awaken to a due sense of the im- portance of deliberate discussion upon all matters per- taining to and having a bearing directly or indirectly upon agriculture. If they would only do this the, would elicit much information that would be URAL erroneous ideas would be dispelled, and valuable mutua, co-operation and assistance would be derived; while at the same time they would be able:to arrive at more desir- able and intelligent conclusions upon matters of the most vital importance to their own welfare. To attend a society of the kind, say once a week in the evening, would be time well spent; it would bring out our young orators and men of ability, and thus provide us with a class of men of whom we are lamentably deficient at present—men who could .efficiently represent us in any public capacity, notably as members of Parliament, and thus look after our interests in, the legislature.—Agri- cultural Gazette.- TKO SHIRJ3 HORSE SOCIETY AND TEE PRESTON Snow.— The annual meeting of the Shire Horse Society was held on Wednesday week, in London. Mr. Gilbey proposed: —"That the members of the Shire Horse Society deplore the alteration in the Preston Shak' prize list of the Royal Agricultural Society's meeting, by adding the words or agricultural' to the classes after the word 'Shire,' and they earnestly hope that in future prize lists the classes may be confined to the 'Shire' breed, as by the addi- tional words or agricultural' foreign buyers are liable to be misled." He said they could scarcely imagine sitting round that table how greatly the decision of the Royal Agricultural Society might affect the Shire bated, because the foreign papers reported what was done at the meetings of the leading society, and reproduced what was printed in the English agricultural papers. The influence of the action of the Royal Soctety thus ex- tended very widely, and if some notice were not taken of the matter he dui not think they would be faithful members of the Shire Horse Society. He thought their decision was open to great objection in Withholding prizes to the most ancient breed of cart-horses in the country, and a breed from which all the other breeds had emanated. (Cheers.) He thought the success of this Society fully bore out everything they might wish to see the Itoyal carry out in connection with this breed. —Mr. J. Martin endorsed everything Mr. Gilbey had said. He thought the resolution should stand by itself, and not be included in the general report.—Mr. Coke expressed his approval of this view, and it was agreed to acccordingly. .-'44aa 'll " LORD TOLLEMACHE'S COTTAGERS.m-We have received says the Daily News, several inquiries, suggested by an article published under this heading., Our correspon- dents are much interested in the description given of the happy state of affairs on Lord Tollemache's estate, but they all conclude, as in a chorus, with the pertinent question, "But how does the cottager get the cow ?" The reply is that he gets it as best he can. The cow clubs, it must be remembered, are for insurance against loss. Whether some fund might be included for the advance of purchase money is, we think, a subject that might well be considered. It has, as a matter of fact, been often discussed, with the conclusion that the cot- tager's independence, and a fair start in cote-keeping, will be best ensured by the habits of thrift by which alone the animal is first acquired. With regard to the particular inquiry quoted above, we may give the follow- mg extract of a letter from a Cheshire gentleman who lives upon Lord Tollemache's estate.—" The acquiring of the cow by the cottager is managed in various ways. In most cases when an agricultural lass and lad con- template matrimony they set about saving some of their yearly earnings, and if 'they have a prospect of acquiring a cow-keeping cottage, it acts as an incentive to increased frugality, with the result that they can generally buy a Cow with their joint fortunes. If they are not in a position to buy a valuable cow they some- times buy an in-calf two-year-old heifer, and if their means will not admit of even this they perhaps buy a couple of one-year-old calves, and graze them for a year,

ke'eping the most promising as a milker, and selling the other. I have often known the farmer for whom the cottager works lend him a pound or two to make up the cost of the first cow, and wait for repayment until the calf was sold. Sometimes lam almost at a loss to know how a man with several children does get his first cow, but I always observe that if he once gets it his comforts and prosperity are manifestly greater from that time." - -

A NHW Home grow.—To the general and long- establiihed Horse Show held in the sumrrier at the Agri- cultural Hall, and the Shire Horse Exhibition annually devoted to the equine beasts of burden, is now added, as a periodically recurring event, the show of the Hack- ney Stud Book Society. The first opened on Tuesday under Royal favour. Small as it necessarily must be, there has been for many years no more interesting show to ,the connoisseur in hackneys, roadsters, cobs, and ponies. The Hackney Stud Book Society was consti- tuted in 1883, was incorporated in January, 1884, for the special purposes of improving the breeds just specified, for compiling and publishing a stud book, and for hold- ing shows. 'Volume I. of the Stud Book has been already been published, and VoL 11. will be issued in a day or two; the members number 370; and the first show now being held is exceptionally good in quality. This is a capital beginning. The society has ample reason to be satisfied with its di/nit in the Agricultural Hall. There are 90 hackney, cob, and pony stallions, 30 thorough- bred sires added by permission of the Council, and a number of army remounts exhibited by H.R.H. the Field-Marshal Commanding, to show breeders the type of horse required for artillery and military engineering purposes. The hackney stallion prizetakers were—in the bigger class, Mr. Flander's Reality Ist, Mr. H. Moore's Confidence 2nd, and Mr. T. Reed's County Member 3rd; In the class between 143 and 15.2 hands, Mr. Burnham's Lord Derby the Second Ist, Mr. S. Rose's Lord Bang 2nd, and the Stand Stud "Company's Star of the East 3rd. 2110, puny stallion prizes were :---Captain Thomaa'a Pomfret Wonder Ist, Mr. Burdett-Coutts' Tommy 2nd, and Mr. W. H. Smith's England's Beauty 3rd. The prizes in the three-year-old hackney horses were :—Mr. Flet- cher's Wildfire Ist and R. Peacock and Son's Vigorous 2nd. Wildfire and County Member are both sons of Mr. Burnham's Lord Derby the Second, which also took a first prize, and the three are wonderfully handsome dark brown animals with fine action. There were two classes of thoroughbreds, including such well-known hunters as theTsteeplechaier Charles L; Pedometer, which fetched:2, ,500, guineas *is a yearling; Soot Guard, the gallant hurdle-racing grey; arid Peppermint. The Hackney Stud Book has been ably edited. It contains the pedigrees of 948 stallions bred in England since 1755, arranged :chronologically and alphabetically, and there is a most:interesting introductory essay, treating of the names, the character, sad the history of trotting horses from the earliest times.

"ENGLAND IN 1985." Monday evening a lecture was given in connection ith the Warrington Co-operative Society in the Co- *iterative Efall, by the Rev. W. Tnekwell, rector of Stock- ton, near Rugby, on "The New Utopia; or England in 1955." The Mayor presided, and there was a very laree attendance,

The MAYOR having briefly introduced the lecturer, The Rev. W. Trcievenere said that 370 years ago the England of our forefathers was heaving under an excite- ment akin to that which agitated us to-day. It was a period known in history as the Renascence—the revolt of will and imagination and life and thought against 15 cen- turies of imprisonment, spreading rapidly from art and lit- erature to regions social, politieal, and religious, awakening a new intellectual and moral force, before which, as it seemed, old distinctions must melt away, the sorrows of the many be relieved, the tyrannies of the few be confounded, the golden age return of brotherhood, of freedom, and of happiness. Foremost amongst the men whom the Reuse- canoe bred was the great Lord Chancellor, Sir Thomas More, and the daring revolutionary spirit of the times was con- densed in his famous romanoe of" Utopia," in which, for the first time in English history, he dealt with problems such as were eonfronting them to-day, problems of capital and la- betas, of crime, of government, of conscience, and of reli- gion. Having recited the preface to More's "Utopia," the lecturer gave a brief outline of the famous story. Read- ing it the other day, he continued, for the fiftieth time, he entertained himself with considering with how little modification it was applicable to the present time. Four hundred years ago, he thought, thisgreat man laid his finger ;As the very sores through which at the present day our body social was suffering. If some of his remedies were fan- tistioal and impossible, he had to consult and consider the caprice of a despotic monarch. With us these proposals were made gravely and practically, for they appealed to the -Irreeistible suffrage of a people whose interest in the exori- meet was vital. Could it be, be (the lecterer) thought to himself, that the certain was destined to rise upon a new Utopia, in which the unfulfilled prophecies of the old shall find consummation and achievement; that the chimera of past centuries is to become the truism et the next; that that power, which in the physical world still brings cosmic life and order out of chaotic disseverance and confusion, had sent forth its fiat to resolve the groanings and the sorrows which rise from the oppressed to-day into the harmony of universal brotherhood, universal knowledge, and universal happiness ?" (Applause.) As he pondered these things his mind became con- fused, past, present, and future were intermingled, and his reverie changed into a dream. He found himself in the little village in which he had spent the last few years of his life. It was the same, yet not the same. The western bills still bounded the horizon in the early summer sunshine. The grey church tower still arose amongst the trees, but all else was strangely altered, and he realised with delight, but without surprise, for one was never surprised in dreams, that the fondest fancy of his life was accom- plished, and that he was allowed to re-visit after a century had passed, the home is which he had lived on earth and to note the changes which time bad made. The cottages which formed the village streets had disappeared, and in- steed of them as far as the eye could reach it rested on gar- den-like enclosures of various sizes, each with a dwelling- house in its midst. Here and there rose stately public buildings, carriages passed to and fro without any visible means of locomotion; a man and a woman whom he en- countered and who appeared not to see him, though attired in working clothes, yet wore costumes far more picturesque than any he remembered, and bore in their manner and countenances and speech the stamp which we associate with education and refinement. As he sauntered wonderingly along his eye and his step were arrested by a particularly interesting group in a garden belonging to a,ssalll farm- house which was the centre of a considerable enclosure of perhaps 20 titres of land. The family consisted of father, mother, and children, ranging from 10 to 20 years old, who were all breakfasting nnder the shade of a tall tree. The father of the family BINV that he was a stranger and invited him in and offered to show him his house. The ground floor of the house was divided in the middle by a curtain into two compartments. One of these compartments was evidently the dwelling parlour of the family. - The walls were beautifully painted by the hands, the man told him, of his children; low bookcases filled with books ran along two sides of the room, and on them stood pictures, statues, vases, and other kinds of ornaments. An instrument re- sembling an organ was in a corner with a flute and violin beside it. On the table were a microscope and spectroscope, prizes, he was told, which had been won at college by one of the sons. The door opened into a em dl conservatory filled with fragrant exotics whose odour perfumed the room. On entering the kitchen he saw no fireplace, but there was a series of cooking pans arranged on a sort of platform by the window. His host informed him that an electrical machine beneath the floor was the motive power which cooked the dinner, warmed and lighted the house, carried hot water to the kitchen parlour and conservatory, and ground the corn in a small mill outside and baked the bread in the oven. (Applause and laughter.) Having described the mode of cultivating this imaginary farm, the lecturer said he was informed by this Utopian farmer that the rent he paid was £2O a year, being £1 an acre, which he paid to the State. (Hear, hoar.) His eon had just returned from. college with a silver medal, and he was delighted to think that the property would continue in the family. Being asked for an explanation of his, he said that the govern- ment had established agricultural colleges, through which every man who wanted land from the State had to pass, there being no other way in which land could be rented. A man who obtained a gold medal at the end of two years' training was allowed to rent 50 acres, a silver medallist. 20 acres, a bronze medallist 10 acres, and a man who obtained a plain certificate 5 acres. The poor fellows who. were "plucked " at their examination had to put up with 2 acres. Every workman employed in manufactures through- out the land had a right to demand of Government one acre on which his house might be built. (Hear, hear.) He asked what was the smallest holding of land on which a man could live, and he was told ten aeres. With five acres a man bad some leisure and with two acres a man had a good deal. Hatay also followed trades as smiths, carpenters, bricklayers, and others worked at the co-operative stores. (Hear, hear.) Work was abundant and wages were high, and every man was well-housed comfortable and independent. A hundred years ago, he was told, in 1885, their village records told them their land supported less than 130 families with a population of less than 700 souls; much land was uncul- tivated, there was innoh wasted by a foolish system of fallowing, many 'lenses were foul, many men were sank in ignorance, poverty, and drunkenness, and all of them were over-worked. Now the same land supported 400 families with a population of 2,000 souls, the houses were comfor- table and even beautiful, the men _were educated and , happy, every square foot was cultivated to its utmost, and cultivated for the sake of those who cultivated it. , (Ap- plause.) His host next referred him to the parson, who, he said, gave them nearly all their lectures, managed their store, he was their chief librarian, the manager of their art gallery, and was besides the best cricketer and best dancer in the parish. (Laughter.) A change then came o'er the spirit of his dream and he found himself in the presence of I the parson. Having told him he was a stranger, and having asked him to first explain to him what his (the parson's) own position was, and how the church and parson were re- concilable with that new world. One hundred years ago, the parson said, the state church represented one religious body, older indeed and more venerable than most of the sects but representing less than one-half of the population, and in its exclusiveness absolutely inconsistent with democratic sentiment. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Yet, it seemed that a state church brought into harmony with public feeling was a potential system for teaching and civilising not to be wantonly thrown away; and that its time-honoured machinery and its many beautiful churches ought if possible to be retained end utilised. It was decreed accordingly that saving the vested interests of existing in- cambents the property of the church should be from that moment the property of the state—(applause)—and that men of all existing sects should be eligible to the state church ministry—(applause) ; that no religious test should be exacted except a solemn profession of Christianity ; that all candidates must pass successfuly a severe examina- tion in science, art, literature, and history ; and that no one could be appointed without the goodwill of two-thirds of the inhabitants Of the district. (Applause.) A good stipend I and a high social position made the post a tempting one and candidates from all sects as well as from the old state church poured in in numbers. At that time those ministers were the ablest men in England, in every sense leaders of their congregations, the churches were multiplied and well filled, the sects were dying out and non-religious bodies were won by the spectacle of a Christianity which was at once national and vital. Speculative theology was extinct and worship had taken its place. (Applause. He (the lecturer) was then shown through the church which was twice the size he remembered it to be. Inside it was aglow with beauty, every window was stained, every foot of surface was coloured, and every capital was carved. From the church they went into the churchyard, and an equal change had taken place there. The old drooping shapeless head- stones which he remembered lied disappeared, velvet paths of turf led among beds of roses of a size and beauty which he, a veteran rose grower, never remember' to have seen. The custom of burying, he was informed, had long been disused. Solemnly and with reverent religious rites their dead were burned and the small residuum of ashes was col- lected and placed beneath the ground and above it a rose tree was planted. (Hear, hear.) The school, which was larger than any board school he had ever seen in London or Manchester, was next described. These schools were supported by the endowment of all the old public schools throughout the country, and were besic:es liberally en- dowed by the State, which gave to them more freely and with more satisfaction than to any other source of outlay. Their next visit was to what his friend called the " Christ" house, by which he soon found that the hospital was meant, and afterwards they went to the village Union, which was a larger and statelier building than he had seen before,anci stood in an enclosure of 18 acres of land. As they passed into the stone entrance of the hall be there be- held two marble statues, whose lineaments seemed to him strangely familiar. One was that of a man aged and erect, tall, with scattered locks of hair round an elevated brow, with deep lines upon the face and wielding an axe in his right hand. (Applause.) The other was that of a younger and slighter man, buttoned closely in the hideous costume of the period, the semblance of an eyeglass dangling from his neck and a sculptured flower in his button hole. (Laughter.) He was told that these were men who were reverenced in England, one as the founder of democracy, and the other as having shaped and guided it thioueh its early difficult stages. (Applause.) They then visited the art gallery and museum,

div.head: MANAGEHENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEHENT OF POULTRY.
FOWLS FOR LAYING PURPOSES.

At the prosent time of the year, we are often met with he question,'" What are the hest fowls for laying pur - poses?" Those who ask this question are generally new beginners in poultry-keeping, or those who have, per- haps, kept fowls, but paid little or no attentiOn to their breed or qualities. They have made the very common error of regarding all fowls as alike, and thought one hen as good as another. It needs:no words of ours to point out the extreme foolishness of this. If a man wanted to buy a horse, and simply purchased the first one he came across, without regard to its capabilities to the work required of it, only asking that it should be cheap, we should regard hi ra as well, not a wise man. And even- if we accept Carlyle'a ill-tempered dictum that there are so many. millions of people in England, mostly fools, we should think this man had a great deal more than big share.of foolishness. • When there are provided to our hands such a variety of breeds, many of which have some special characteristic, it does seem the height of foolishness to refuse the expenditure of a little thought and consideration, such as would secure that which will be best for the purpose in view. The expenditure of time and thought need not be very great, for there are at hand all the important breeds, and they can be obtained at a reasonalsie cost, either by the pur- chase of stock birds, or sittings of eggs. Both these methods of procuring fresh stock can be reeommended. But the purchase of eggs is sometimes risky, unless the seller is known either personally or by repute. We hove previously given descriptions of the various breeds of laying fowls, but as yearly there are new readers of The Guardian, as every season finds some one else wishful to "go in" for poultry keeping, and as the necessities of agricultural life impel,, the choice of new ways of procedure, we have sometimes to travel a little over trodden; ground. The reason for this will be ob- vious, and it may be that herein will be something of service.to older readers of this column.

The development of different breeds would be a very interesting study were it poiale to make it,but so much is due to natural selection, to climatic influences, and to other circumstances, that there would be in- volved many difficulties almost impossible to overcome. In consequence however, of these_ varying conditions, we find nearly fifty breed; and varieties of poultry, each more or less distinct from the other. -These are to be classified into four great divisions. First, the non. sitting breeds; second, the sitting varieties; third, the generally useful breeds; and fourth, the fancy varieties. Some of these run one into the other, especially the second and third divisions, but with the:so we do not now propose to deal, as we only wish to indicate the members of the 'first. .

--It-i-s-Woirafifoift-t7o see that Where the primary object is the production of eggs, the non-sitting varieties have a very: manifest advantage over others. Maternal duties, though most important for the reproduction of the species, take a large slice. out of the year and tell heavily upon the egg basket. If a hen sits three weeks, and then goes with the chickens six more before re- awning her laying, we may say there are ten weeks gone, for there are sure to be a few days before she is placed upon a nest. This repeated twice in the year, with six weeks for moulting, means six months when she is unproductive, so far as eggs are concerned. The non-sitting hen, asking only the moulting time for rest, has 20 more weeks during which she can lay, and is thus able to foot up a much greater total. It has been claimed that the sitting period is necessary for preserving the hen's strength. So it may be in the case of the heavier breeds, but from a long experience of non-sitters, we can safely say tfiat they are able to lay 45 weeks out of the 52, and be as fresh at the end of that time as others that have only layed 25 week. What one man can do another oannot. What is easy to one is hard to another. And in this case "it is their nature to," which with every species of living thin is sufficient explanation for such differences as there are. `Mere is a good choice amongst varieties of non-sitters, but the best of these are of the races owing their origin to the races found on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea. We are accustomed to class all these as Spanish, but this is an error, and the division made on the Con- tinent, namely, Spanish and Italian fowls, Is more cor- rect. In the former are included Black Spanish, Minor- cas, and Andalusians, and in the latter all the colours of Leghorns. Those, together with Houdans and Polish, comprise the non-sitting division of domestic poultry. Among the Spanish varieties we place the black Minorcas first. These need no recommendation at our hands. They are well known in this district, and many readers of The Gaardian can testify to their value as layers. We hope that everyone who keeps them will endeavour to develop their laying properties, by breed- ing from the best layers only, of course, regarding such considerations as type, size, and hardiness. Andalusians come next, and they are hardly less fecund, but are scarcely so pleasing in appearance. The black Spanish at one time were the par excellence of all laying fowls, but they have been spoiled by breeding for the white face. Still, with the expenditure of a little care, they might in a few years be restored to their old position. How this could be done, we need not.) now say. But it is possible, and would well 'repay anyone taking them up with this object in view. Of the Leghorns, the best are the -whites, but the others are nearly as kood: Houdans are a splendid fowl, especially on farms, and are mneh better on the table than are any of the others. Polish we have dealt with so recently that we need not say more about them now. It is not a little remarkable that all the non-sitters, except the black Spanish, are hardy, and bear confine- ment very well. Thus they are suitable both for farmers and those whose space is limited. They have the fault already noted, namely, that they are, with the exception of the Houdan, not very good on the table. Of course all are passable as chickens, but even then are rather dig in flesh. But their extraordinary fecundity quite makes up for this failing. Unfertile eggs are at all times a great annoyance to the poultry keeper, and every effort should be put forth for their prevention. A frequent cause is that the male bird has not sufficient food, even though there be an abun- dance put down to him. The reason is that some gallant cocks will not eat Until their hens are all satisfied, and unless the feeder notices this fact he will give over sup- plying food when they have had enough, and the cock has to go without. If this be suspected, he should be closely watched, and if what we have stated is found to be the case, feed apart from the hens after they are done. This may entail a little trouble, but it is neeeqsary. He may also haves little meat now and again.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

FRU/T PROSPECTS.—Judging from the appearance of the buds on all kinds of fruit trees, there is a good pros- pect of an excellent fruit season. The exceptionally warm summer we have had was most favourable to the production of fresh bud, and the maturing of the wood On all the trees. Considering the prevailing open weather we have had the buds are in a backward con- dition, and for that reason have a better chance of escaping late frosts which, in the majority of season's, occasion more or lessiaavoq.amongst: the fruit blossom. The latter part of last week the land was drying up nicely on the surface, and up to Tuesday we had hopes of being able to commence preparing some of it by forking it over six or eight inches deep, and hastening the drying process. Since then the rain has well soaked the ground once more. If this operation of turning over the soil can be performed on one of those sunny days we may expect to visit us now we are in March, we shall increase the temperature of the soil by turning that part that has been warmed by the sun underneath, and ex- • posing more to be warmed. This will have a marked effect on the young crops, which are as often retarded by the coldness of the soil as by that of the atmosphere. Loosening the soil permits the water to pass down more freely, which of itself increases the warmth of the soil. Wet or water-logged soil is well-known ttolbe much colder than the dry and porous. The plots that will re- ceive our attention first will be those intended for par- snips, onions, beans, and peas. Those who are in the habit of using sticks for the latter should secure a stock at once, and prepare them by pointing the thick end, so they may readily enter the soil;. and their sides should be trimmed so as to give them a flattened appearance. The trimmings, that may be a foot or so in length, should be saved, as they may come in handy to put to the peas when a few inches above the soil, which is much preferable to placing the large sticks to them at that early stage. THE FRONT GARDEN.—There arc several things at the present time pushing their growth just alicve the soil that should be carefully watehed in case they are eaten by slugs. If there are any indications of the presence of these pests, we would advise that a few handfuls of soaked bran or brewers' grains be laid about at once, and if these are examined at night, with the aid of •a lamp, most of the slugs will be found feeding on them, and they may be picked off, or the material and them moved bodily away and replaced by some fresh. The plants that suffer most :are Pyrethrums, Rudbeekias, Campanulas, Centranthes, and Rockets, and amongst plants in a more advanced stage will be found Pansies, Violas, and Carnations. From some favoured localities we hear that several plants are in flower, such as Aubretias, Crocus, Scilla Sibrica, Stocks, Polyanthus, Violets, and Christmas roses or Hellebores. We have only seen the two latter and some Crocuses in flower in the neighbourhood of Preston this season yet. Of Christmas roses there are several varieties, some having pure white flowers; and, considering that the plants are perfectly hardy, it is surprising that they are not grown more extensively. If they are lifted and placed in pots in a cold frame, they become veritable Christmas roses, as many will flower at that festive season when so treated. We feel sure that they would do well in the ' windows if lifted and potted in October. ROSES, unlike the fruit trees, are in an unusually for- ward condition, and many will be tempted to prune them, but we advise them to exercise caution, and defer general pruning for a week or two. Those who grow a quantity of roses prune in batches, at intervals of a week or more, with the view of having suenessional bloom as well as escaping the influence of frost on all the young growth. If the roses were pruned maw it is obvious that the latent buds at the base would be forced at once into growth by the upward rush of sap, and be- tween now and April they could scarcely escape tho frost. We learn from a contemporary that Mr. Evans, of Itowlandville, Philadelphia, has secured from Mr: Bennet, of Shepperton, his two new seedling roses, "William Fraser Bennet" and "Her Majesty," for the sum of £1,600! Mr. Bennet is well known amongst rosarians as a successful hybridiser of roses. THE WixDow.—Cyclamen persicum : Few persons are aware that the plants which Mr. Wilding and others show so well at the Preston and Fulwood spring Exhibi- tion are nearly hardy, and for that reason are suitable for the cottager who has no glass protection. We saw recently a plant that had been in% cold frame during the most severe frosts we have had this season and the corms and soil must have been frozen, but the plant was in perfect health, and showing some dozens of flowers. After the flowering season is over water must be gradu- ally withheld, and after all the leaves turn yellow they will not require any till they get thoroughly dry. To- wards the end of May or early in June they may be turned out of doors and the pots placed on their sides, in which position they may remain till they show signs of growth.
Public Analysts have submltted CADBURY'S CCCOI to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt.

CAI3INET COUNCIL —A Cabinet Council was held on Saturday. The chief subject of deliberation was the Rae. Sian advance towards Herat. Ministers were assisted in their councils by further despatches from Sir Peter Lumsden. After the Council rose, Musurus Pasha had a private con- ference with Earl Granville. PROPOSED NEW OFFICIAL RESIDENCE FOR THE PREMIER. —Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Lord Rosebery, Lord R. Grosvenor, Mr. Childers, and Mr. H. Gladstone, left Down- ing-street on Saturday, and walked over to Dover House, where they were met by Mr. Mitford and Mr. Thompson, of the Office of Works. A complete inspection was made of the house with a view to its being taken as a residence for the Premier. It is probable that it will be bought for the official residence of future English Premiers. Cams that the line would be opened for through traffic in the course of 1887 or 1888. In reply to a further question put by Sir Henry, Lord E. It would be presented in the form , of a resolution for the foundation of a bill to obtain guarantees. SCPPLY.—The House then went into Committee of Sup- ply on the Civil Service Estimates. Towards midnight the Pante NitntsTrin joined in the debate, and referring to some re- marks of Mr. Onslow, the right hon. gentleman said he was not prepared to admit that the friendship of any country in the world was necessary or even had been necassary te en- able this country to maintKin its position.—A supplemen- tary estimate for £B9O for Irish pauper lunatics led to some discussion on the condition of pauper lunatics in Irish work- houses.—The Committee divided—For the reduction, 22; against 61.—The vote was then agreed to. The other orders having been disposed of, the House ad- j )8 rned.

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.

SCUOOL EX&MINATION —The Wesleyan day school ex- amination at Irlam took place on the Id iota, when 123 children were presented. The following passed :—Reading 41, writing 28, arithmetic 35, total 104 ; 19 failed. This is a fair average, and reflects great credit on Mrs Nutter, the school teacher. The sewing of the girls was of a high character, and well deserve the commendation it received.

Misstow hERVICBS.—The Rev T Riley. district mission- ary, paid a visit on Sunday, when the chapel was crowded both morning and evening. The rev gentleman preached two most impressive sermons. On the Monday evening there was a tea in the schoolroom, which was well attended. At the close Mr Riley conducted a singing band through the street into the chapel, which was again filled to overflow- ing. The resident minister, Rev R Dillon, 7received into the church a little over 100 on trial, followed by an appropriate address. Mr Riley brought the service to a close by an effective address.

United Ireland expresses the satisfaction of the Irish people at Dr. Walsb's election as dignissimus for the Archbishopric of Dublin, and says he never has been a violent politician. News has come from America that Patrick Egan, presi- dent of the Irish League, received at a ball a parcel, which his son opened and found to contain a dynamite machine, regulated for explosion. At Burnley, on Thursday, Thomas Callagher was com- mitted for trial for haying wounded his wife by stabbing her saveral times about the forehead with a common ttble- fork whilst she lay in bad asleep. The Mayor of Blackpool on Thursday Dlaced the first rail of an electric tramway which is to be laid along the whole length of the Promenade. It is expected that the cars will be at work by Whit-week. .

A VIOLENT PRISONER.—On James Lee, charged with tbe murder of Inspector Simmons, being remanded at Romford on Thurrthy, be became very violent, and to be handcuffed before being removed to the cells. _ _

THE STOKE NEWINGTON MYSTERY.—A woman named Eliza Salmon was arrested at Romford on Wednesday night, charged on suspicion with having murdered her little girl, about four years eld, by drowning, at Stoke Newington.
