----- WIDNES (2SD TEAM V. OTJONTRINOTON.—TheSe two teams met at the ground, Lowerhouse-lane, Widnes, on Saturday, and a fair number of spectators witnessed the pro- ceedings. After a long game the play resulted as follows: —Widnes, nine minor points, two tries, and a goal from a disputed try to nil. The Widnes team was composed of the following :—Full back, Pennington; backs, Bedgood, Wright, Ogden, Cornfield, Chritnes ; half backs, Brown, Rey, Samp- son ; forwards, Spencer, Woods, Wilkinson, Davies, Barton. For the Widnea team Pennington played well. Good play was also shown by Brown, Sampson, Woods, and Spencer. Ireland, the captain, did good work on behalf of the Ought- rlnsrton team. RUNCORN OLD BOYS V. MOSS BANK WHITS STAR (Wimine).—This match wee played on the ground of the rlatter on Saturday afternoon. The day was. fine, and a ;friendly and pleasant game took place, resulting in a win ['for the home team, the score beieg—Moss Bank. two tries '(obtained by Flinn) and two minor points; Old Boys. one °try (obtained by W E C Harvey) and three minor points. The teams were as follosys :—Old Boys: Full back, W Catterall ; three-quarter backs, W Wiehlade, F H Harvey, and W Tickle; half backs, J Prince and B Williams; f or- wards, W E C Harvey, Shaw, S Abram., W Shaw, E ',Howard, P Shaw, T Knight, d Steele, and Higgins. Moss Bank Fall back, W Winton, three-quarter backs, Lomax, piton (oaptainl, and Boyle; half backs, Barker and Devitt; forwards, Sauce, Hewitt, Murty, Whelan, McKeowin, Crosby, Eastwood, McManus, and Daffy. Sr. HELENS RECREATION V. ST. HELENS—These Old rivals played their return match on the ground of the former on Saturday in the presence of over six hundred spectators, the proceeds being for the benefit of James Parr, who was hurt whilst playing for the Recreation against Litherland. A hard game resulted in a victory for the visitors by two goals, one try, and one minor point to One goal, one try, and four minor points. The Recreation got two other tries which were disallowed by the referee. Ruskin and Gregson got the tries for the Recreation and Finney aud Halton for St. Helena Green, Pyke, and Langley played a splendid game for the Recreation, whilst Borthwick and Halton played very well for the "Saints." Teams :—St. Helen-It T G Rogers, back ; A Tickle, W C Haseldon, and J Greg; son, three-quarter backs ; T Finney (captain) and .1 Edwards, half-backs; C Anders, A Borthwicb, W James, T Pennington, J Basnett, If Unsworth, J Halton, .1 Har- wood, and It F 8 Twist, forwards. Recreation : W E Tay- lor, back ; J Seddon, Pike, and R Langley, three-quarter backs; P Roberts and T Rankin, half-backs ; P Finn, "Mousey " (captain), T Green, W Cook, H Gregson, Dean, J Hankinson, Fletcher, and Higham, forwards. Nxerrox v. Vuxcerr.—These two rival local Rigby clubs met in a friendly contest on Saturday on the ground of the first named. The proceeds of the match were for the benefit of the parent of a late member of the Newton club. The splendid weather and the charitable object of the match at- tracted no less than 1,500 people, who were rewarded by witnessing a splendidly contested ga.ne. The turf was in good condition, and therefore favoured a fast game. The general opinion seemed to be that this was the best match that has been played at Newton for some time, the back play of the Vulcan, especially their passing, being much admired, and when "No aide" was called, Newton was de- clared the winners of a very fast and exciting, but pleasant, game, the score being one goal (dropped by W Lane), one try (W Mee), and three minor points, to Vulcan two tries (J Wuhliamt and J Nicholls), and one minor point. For Newton Messrs W Lane, J Astall, G Lane, W Mee, T Brad- dock, T Egan, jour, and R Elitchen were most prominent, and the William's, Nicholls, Varley, and Wright played well for Vulcan. Mr E T Parry ably officiated as referee. Teams: Newton: G Lane, back ; W Mee, J Astall, and J Board- man, three-quarter backs ; W Lane and T Egan, junr., half-backs; W Pennington, T Braddock, W Rose, T Egan, sem., J Naylor, A Latimer, S Rimmer, R Hitchin, and T Fairclougb, forwards. Vulcan : A Williams, back ; J Williams, %V Prescot, and S Williams, three-quarter backs ;1 T Massey and J Varley, half-backs; II F Gooch (captain), F W Bolton, T Owen, R Wright, J Prescot, W Blair, J Nicholls, R Sherlock, and J Naylor, forwards. BARLESTOWN V. FISHWICH RAMBLERS (PRESTOIS).—Af ter winning the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup and gold medals on the previous Saturday, the Earlestown team sus- tained a severe reverse on Saturday last. Their opponents were Fishwick Ramblers a strong organisation from Pre- ton, and they included n their ranks Gillespie and Damp-

g the famous North End Club. The Liverpool Cap hjia„B 5, resented by their full team with. Vet ez.e.ejlt tion of Ogden, whote plee7 was filled by FergusOn, of the 2nd eleven. There was a large alte'udlnce of spectators who manifested a great interest in the OW. Balling won the toss, the Earlestoniana elected to pley uphill geed with the wind in their favour in the first half. Dempsey started the leather for the Ramblers, who played exceedingly well throughout the game. Their passing was greatly superior to that of the Earlestoniane and their combized play was warmly applauded. Up to hat-time the play was very even, but the visitors displayed a greater brilliancy in front el goal than their opponents. The home forwards were evi- dently out of form, and when ends were changed the score was Ramblers four goals, Earlestown one. Shortly after the resumption of play the Fishwick team notchee a filth goal amidst applause. The Earlestonians still played in a loose fashion, and their supporters rained repeated cries of " play up, Earlestowe." The shouts appeared to rouse them, and for the last half-hour they very severely pressed their opponents. The Prestonians were comnelled to act on the defensive, and their goal was many a time seri- ously endangered. The home team had the best of the game in the second half, but they failed to draw level with the score of the visitorn. When time was called the Earle!. town team retied defeated (for the second time in 19 matches) by five goels to three. The teams were :—Earles- town J Appleton, goal ; R Green and J Green, backs ; R P.3.wker, Duxbury, and J Whalley, half-backs ; W R;ch and J Ellieon, right wing; A W Dagnall, certre ; .1 Sims and T Ferguson, left wing. Fishwack Itamblere J Addi- son, goal ; R Entwistle and T Baverstock, backs ' • J C Clitheroe and T Cornell, half-backs ; A Saul and W Lamb, right wing; A Dempsey, Centre; J Gillespie and A Green- wood, left wing. linoraerrow v. ViraRIIISTOTOST.— A date being vacant on the Broughton list on Saturday, arrangements were made for a fifteen to visit Warrington with the double object of giving an exposition of the Rugby game by a first-class team, and giving a lift to the local club at the same time. Ac- cordingly a teem, captained by T Doane, met the Warring- ton contingent on their own ground. The afternoon being beautifully tine, a concourse of something like 2,500 specta- tors witnessed the game, whichin the first half was altogether in favour of Broughton, who scored a goal and a try to nil. In the second half only minor points were scored, and these were in favour of Warrington, who undoubtedly bad the beat of the play, but never could manage to get in a win- ning mark, although on several occasions they were very near doing it. Tho game throughout was a capital one, terminating in a victory for the visitors by one goal, one try, to Warrington four minor points. The visiting captain started the bell shortly before halfpest three, against a Cross wind. Barnes made a slight return, and after a line out a long punt by the same player sent the ball into touch near the centre. Jordan and Prince removed play to the home 25 flag, where a very long and stiff scrimmage took place. From this the ball was passed to Maesev, who failed to hold it; Jordan then picked up and ran in between the poste, kicking a goal from the place. Eater the restart 10030 play took place, mostly about midfield. A long and very stoutly contested pack followed, Warrington having the hest of it, and Massey again unfortunately failed to handle the ball when passed to him, and, as in the former instance, Jordan, being in close attendance, got possession and relieved his side. Gilbert was next con.picerous with a goad dribble, and then from near midfield Deneett mode a 'tieing run through his opponents, passing in time to Arthur Evans, who safely crossed the line, Jordan failing at goal. No- thing more was scored up to half time. After change of ends Frank Turner restarted, and play went on at a very fast rate, and before long Brouehton had to save. There was a very noticeable falling off in the vigorous play shown by the visitors in the earlier part of the game, and a second touchdown was scored againet them Deena strong inn by Dilloei was spoiled by Deenett forcing him to touch in goal. whileehlassey compelled a third tenchdown; the gerna finishing with the result stated- above. The arie all throughout was very pleasant, and in the second half great- ly in favour of Warrington, for whom Speakman, Warren, Gilbert, Rigby, and Dillon played vary well. On the other side Deranett and Jordan were the pick of the back division, the full beck particularly playing with great judgment and coolness. Teams :—Brooghton : IV Dannett, back ; F Prince, James Kneen, and E Jordan. three-quarter backs ; T Deane (captain), and D Graeowool, half-backs ; B U Hearn, P Lodge, E L Evans, H Mudie, A E Evans, Ii Moss, F Wormald, IV R Lombard, and E U Finch, forwards. War- rington : T Walsh. back; IV pei k an, T Barnes, and J I Massey, three-quarter backe; E Gilbert and J E War- ren, half-back.; Fair Turner, H Ashton iciptain), J Jolly, W Povey, J Rigby, E Dillon, Frank Turner, W Hayes, and J Jones, forwards. Umpires, R Metal° and .1 Bramwell ; referee, 1' R Sutton. Itterecorter v. WlClAN.—Considerable interest was taken in the meeting of Wigan and Runcorn at the latter place on Saturday, when about two th msand spectators lined the ropes, and as was anticipated a capital game was witnessed. Joule started what proved to be a fast game. No return to the kick off being effected, Gatley and Linfiland reached the Wigan 25, Andrews kicking in touch. From the line out, Brayshaw and Astley moved in an opposite direction, but the play was soon again in the Wigan quarters, the result of quick and combined forward play. Hard scrim :)aging en- , sued on the line, but the visitors tided over the danger, and Smith made a little headway, but was tackled well by Wain- wright. Johnson followed up with a smart run to Stevie, who rolled him into touch, Anderton 'eeing forced soon after to touch down. Following the drop out, Banks gave Bald- win a chance, but he preferred to kick into the home 25, where the ball rolled touch in goal. The ball having been dropped out Speakman was instantly to the front, and the ball falling to the forwards they rushed over the Wigan line, Barns grounding it and Lewis making a fair attempt at goal. Play being resumed, a very short time elapsed ere the home forwards, playing splendidly together, dribbled up to the line, where Anderton mulled the ball. H Hughes and Gatley being on the track, Hughes sharply secured it, but the kick at goal was again unsuccessful. The ball be- ing again brought oat, play lodged for a short time is the centre, with Speakman constantly on the ball, giving Wain- wright a chance. far which he is ever on the lookout, who in turn threw to Hughes, and some progress was again made. Smith sent the ball to W Hughes, who exchanged to Wainwright. Smith tackling smartly close to the quarter flog. Following the scrimmege, the ball fell to Wainwright, who was anon held by Norris and Mockett, and the former getting a rather [ smart possession of ;the ball before the scritnmag,e was formed or ball played on, crossed the home line. An ap- peal to the referee gave them the try, no goal being kicked. Half time was declared soon afterwards, the game standing Runcorn: Two tries, one minor point ; Wigan : One try, one minor point. After change of ends Brayshaw kicked eff, Johnson making a good return to Smith, who was well collared, the ball going into touch. Wainwright soon after gained ground by kicking in touch well up towards the Wigan line, and by further pressure Wigan were compelled to save. Soon to work again, and Braysleaw started a good dribble, which Speakman promptly stopped, and soon after It felt a) the lot of Johnson and Hughes to stop similar efforts. Gatley and Andrews got tender way nicely, but their object was frustrated by Smith. H Hughes tried to wriggle through, but was effectively met by Norris. From the centre Joule and Lightburn got on along the touch line, gaining considerable headway, 101 l md, Gatley, and Light- barn getting to the line, and the ball going into touch in goal. Speakman getting the ball after the drop out ran well, and shortly afterwards a free kick falling to his lot NV Hughes tried at goal, though it was not successful. An- derton later on was pressed, and drew back and touched down. To the close of the game the play was chiefly cen- tral; a well contested match ending in a victory for Run- corn, viz., two tries, four minor points, to one try and one minor point. The Runcorn forwards never played a better game, their dribbling and smart play being frequently ap- plauded. The backs did theTr work very well, but were short of speed. For Wigan, Slavin, Smith, and Morris be- hind, Brayshaw, Holt, Astley, and Mockett played a hard game. Teams :—Bancorn : IV Hughes, back; Johnson, Speakman, and Wainwright, three-quarter backs; Hughes and Andrews, half backs •, Wright, Joule, Lewis, Clarke Holland, Dean, Barns, Gatley, and Lightburn, forwards: Wigan : Anderton, back; Smith, Beldwin, and Sievin, three-quarter backs; Moms and Books, half backs ; Brayshaw, Astley, Ratter, Mockett, Ingham, Leyland, Prest, and Norris, forwards. Mr Winks, Wavertree F.C., acted as referee.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

Referring to the capital game that came off at Warring- ton on Saturday, between the local team and Broughton, the Athletic News says that it is quite evident Warrington know how to play a good game. Those who have watched the form of the team during the present season, and the sterling way in which they have work2d, will gladly coin- cide with the remark. As might have been foretold, War- rington suffered defeat at the hands of Broughton, but it was an honourable one, and reflects considerable credit on the local men, when the standing of their opponents is considered. The second round of the Yorkshire Rugby Challenge Cup competition was brought to a close on Saturday, and the leading clubs have again made their way into another round. Bradford only succeeded in beating Caatleford after playing an extra half hour, during which time, however, the Brad- ford men scored a goal and two tries to nil. Wakefield Trinity and Halifax only succeeded in gaining minor points against Cleckheaton and Horbury respectively, but as a majority of three minor points in this competition edifices to decide the ties, the two first-named clubs won. Dewsbury, Batley, Leeds St. John's, Manninghatn, and the Halifax Free Wanderers are also among the winners of ties. The seventh international match under Association rules between England and Wales has been arranged to take place on Saturday next, at Blackburn. The previous contests , have resulted in England winning four and losing two, a ' record, considering that the Welsh Association numbers bat 22 clubs and is mainly confined to North Wales, favourable to the Principality. The Yorkshire County Club haa lost no time in making ar- rangements for the next season, and have completed the following fixtures :—November 14, against Durham• ; Nov- ember 21, Northumberland; and November 28, Lancashire. Matches with Cheshire, Middlesex, Surrey, and the Midland Counties will probably be arranged.

Lord Hartington has, it is stated, consented to visit Rai- fast during Whitsuntide, for the purpose of opening the Ulster Reform Club: Mr. Herbert Gladstone, who represents the °Ma, of Works in the House of Commons, will receive a salary of £l,OOO, to commence on the 31st inst. It is said that Lord Randolph C'lnrchill, on his retina from India, will be irwited to contest the Central Division of Sheffield in the Conservative interest. The Queen will not go to Germany until after the 28th the anniversary of the Duke of Mbony's death. No date is yet fixed for the Queea's departure. On Saturday night, a fire occurred at the factory of Messrs John Lowson, Jan., and Go, Forfar, by which dam- age from £lO,OOO to £l5 000 was sustained. Three men who were the originators of the riot, were' each fined .£5,( and the ether six were ordered to.came vine tor jadgenent, when called upon. RAILWAY ACCIDENT—An alarming accident nocnrred on Wednesday on the incline branching off from the Taff Vales Railway, about six miles from Poutypridd. A locomotive with four loaded truck eof coal ran away-about half a tuile.i when it was turned off by a pair of hall pain's, the engine was overturned, the trucks were smaehed, and t':e coal was seattered in all directions. Tee driver, Oceania, and brakes- man jumped off before the engine overturned. Two of the • men were injured. The 'steamers Presiten, Fern maod, and C endon left New York:about the middle of January for English ports, and havS''',Bol since tame hexed of. The Coniston, which sailed Irani Liver- pool for New York on Cbrietmas-eve, is tow tin months overdue. The vessels were owned in Hartlepool, Newcastle, and leondon, THE I.ISWORTH COLLIERY EXPLOSIoN.—The eupooeitiea that fire he'd broken out in the workings at LTeworth Col- liery appears to have been groundless. A oriuncil of mining authorities met on Monday, spent over two boars in the pit, and several gentlemen advanced 100 yards beyond the steppsze. They found ne trace of fire, but the after-damp was too dangerous to allow of their continuing in the tniue. The miners have decided not to return until the bodies have been recovered and the saline put in a safe con- dition. Another death has occurred, thus bringing up the total number to 42. THE MARQUIS OF RIPON'S INDIAN ADMINISTRATIoN.—On Seturday, the Maiquie of Ripon was presented by the lead- ing Indian residents of the Metropois with anaddress of congratulation on the success which had attended his ad- ministration of Indian affairs. His Lordship, in reply, said One main branch of his policy bad been the establtshtntnt of local governing boards, and the whole success or failure of the recent efforts of the Government in India would depend upon the practical working of those boards. He defended the repeal of the Vernacular Press Act, and said nothing would induce them tot e-insoose similar cost- eve legislation—a step only justifiable on the score of public danger. WEST GLOUCESTERSHIRE EascrioN.—The following is the official diaclaration of the poll :—Mr Ankara (C), 4,837 ; Sr W Marling (L), 4,426; majority, 411. At the general elcction in 1880, the polling resulted as follows :—Celonel Riugscote (L), 5,316; Lord Moreton (L), 5 164 ; and Mr Randall Plunkett (C), 4,640; the first two candidates being returned. Mr Ackers said his thanks were due not only te Conservatives, but to many supporters who, although in the past they classified themselves as Liberals, had in this national crisis voted for him as a protest against the policy of the present Government. Sir William Marling and Mr Stanton, M.P., returned thanks on behalf of the Liberals, attributing the defeat to falsehoods circulated by the Con- servatives, especially in charging the Government with be- ing the murderers of Gordon, and said tne victory would be only a short-lived one. THE LONDON DrxinirTis Our at.o sS.— kt Bow-street - Court, London, on Monday, James G. Cunningham AOL,. Henry Burton were again charged with being can the recent dynamite outrages in London. Several wit= were examined concerning the explosion at Vic•orie Station on February 26th, 1881. and the 6adme of metal fragments and portions of clockwork among the debris was deposed to. Proof was adduced of the discovery of a portmanteau crone taming dynamite at Litigate lull and Paddington Stations, and the portmant.an found at the former station was proved to have been purchased in Fleet-street on February 25th, 1884, but the shopman could not identify either of the prisoners as the purchaser. Evidence having been given - as to the occurrence of explosions at the Junior Cerlton Club and Scotland Yard, the discovery of dynamite neat the Nelson column, and the fluding of a crumpled envelope 'in the portmanteau left at Paddington, bearing the name e "Jack Donavan," the prisoners were remanded for a week." The prisoners' solicitor woe accompanied by a member of the New York bar.

The applicant then withdrew Tits ROYAL Yuri* TO IRBLAND.—The arrangements for this visit re now nearly complete. The Prince and Prin. e.se er Wales, Prince Albert Victor, and Prince George of Wales will proceed from Kingstown, on the Bth April, to Dublin Castle. In the afternoon they will visit the Royal Du'Ain Society's Agricultural Show at Ball's Bridge, where an address will be presented by the Duke of Leinster on behalf of the society. On the next day a levee will be held on behalf of the Queen at Dublin Castle. On the fol- lowing day the Prince of Wales will lav the foundation- stone of the Science and Art Museiim at -Kiidare-place, and may visit Lord and Lady Powerscourt at Bray. In the evening there will be a drawing-room and full-dress state ball at Dublin Castle. On Saturday there will be a state banquet at the Castle. If there be not a citizens' ball there will be one given by the principal clubs. The Freemasons of thayeefoirr Irish formed ard lodge. On Monday their Royal Ilighnesees will proceed to .' mer, to a committeespecial to in v coi tale ni theun ricraitnicoet; whoof theis grand patron Convemore near Mallow. whore they will be the guests et , the Earl and Countess of Listowel till the 18th. In the . meantime they will visit Cork, probBbly on Tuesday ; and ' the Marquis of Waterford at Curra,.:hmore on Wednesday. ' On Thursday they will proceed to Killarney, where they will be the guests of the Lord Lieutenant and the Countess Spencer, at whose disposal Lord Kenmare's beautiful resi- dence has bees placed for the occasion. On Dlonday, the 20,h, their Royal Highnesses will return to Dublin and stay at the Viceregal Lodge. They will be present at Punches.. town races, which will be held on the 21st and 22nd April. en the 23rd they will leave Dublin for Belfast, and will pro- bably sleep on board the royal yacht. On Saturday they will visit Derry, and thence proceed to 13aronscourt, where they will be the guests of the Duke of Abercorn. They will afterwards return to Belfast, crossing to Scotland by the Etranraer route. With: ean ADSTONE as anything rosy in connec- , rattle AT. W.ar : for, with Mr. GL • civetr4lellts bei: ng made ridiculous have no fear of these ridiculous by the ills- lak ti of a blunder in the estimates amount- Ilidhich rridil.lieas-:—such, for instance, as that 4rirl ,Liscredited the late Administration „ "11014D,1,`°,.e War in Afghanistan. It is bad Liihi. tor this country to have to pay any- °l; ba.ti.' ta,,lld if Egypt were not on the verge °- thk -lotcy it would certainly be the duty 9 i, th e tr.. -e 1 Ith Government to insist that 104idwht o live in the land of the Pharoahs ',a the D,43' for their own protection. " Spoil- 41Yptians " is a favourite phrase

with a certain class of politicians; but as things go it would seem that the danger is rather that, before current transactions are at an end, the Egyptians will "spoil us. We are not yet ,out or the wood, and we venture to assert that, if the power of the MAIIDI has to, be destroyed at Khat- toum before we can.: leave the Soudan, the sacrifices we have made will be small com- pared with those' we shall be called upon. to make. It is , for this reason that we hail with satisfaction expressions in the speeches of Lord HstaiNGTON ' and the Pant*. Mumma which thow that. It is by no Means absolutely certain that an expedition to Khartoum will be necessary. Lord HARtING- Ton used the words ," probably ultimately necessary," and the Opposition repeated the word 'probably" by way of showing how distasteful to them' was the idea of a possibly peaceful solution of the present difficulties in the Soudan. Mr. GiAnsTONE said, "the question whether the forces were to go to Khartoum," and the declaration he had 'pre- viously made on the subject, formed "a fair subject for quotation and for comment, and he had no doubt there would be a- great deal to be said upon it.at the,proper time." The vote before the House, he added, "related to an expedition with the view, of neutralis- ing the action, or destroying, if necessary, any action of OMAN DroxA—an operation equally necessary whatever view were adopted with respect to the expedition to Khartoum." It would seem, therefore, that the policy of the Government at present dbes not go be- yond giving the "quietus "to Osuxti DIGNA. It is felt that if he were let alone he might become troublesome to the British troops' encamped on the Nile; but, if all that is sought is the security of the Nile column, it is reasonable to urge: that there is no press- ing necessity, to attenpt to lay__ a railway be- tween Sualim and Berber. We say attempt because we are by no means .convinced that the railway will ever be laid. Lord HiRT- INGTON is evidently not very sanguine about its being cohstructed in time to carry troops to Berber daring the next season's opera- tions; but it is urged that whatever portion can be brought into use would be a great advantage. The nation, howevet, looks upon the project as one to connect the Red Sea with the Nile, and if, after a large expendi- ture of money, a portion only can be made available for Military, purposes, it will b felt that the scheme has proved a failure, and the Government will be condemned accordingly. But, taking what on the face of it is the best view of the sitnation, and assuming that the iron road is ultimately made, that Berber is reached, and Khartoum destroyed,' what, it should be asked, is to:be•done then Y The Government are pledged, out and out, to ,the policy of evacuating the Soudan, and- to this end we should have to do one of two things —either take up the line of rails we ha o laid at so much trouble and cost, or leave it to redden with rust in the wilderness. The adoption of either course would lead to a loud outcry, and endanger the position of the. Government. It Worild delight the Tories to have such an opportunity. Eveh now they vapour vaguely about opening up the Soudan to commerce; but if the Soudan were evacuated after constructin,, a railway from the Red Sea to the Nile they would, we must confess, hav-: a good case against the Ministry. It is because we per- ceive this—because we see that staying in the Soudan a day longer than is 'necessary is fraught with the danger of entanglements that will cause usto stay permanently—that we should be glad to hear the Government an- 'nounce' that' the raii*ay scheme was aban- doned, and that no further military operations would be undertaken except such as were strictly necessary for the protection of our soldiers now on the banks of the Nile. There would then be a clear issue before the coun- try. The Opposition, as Mr. GLADSTONE said on-Monday, mean "the reconquest and re- tention-of the Soudan." The present Gov- ernment are definite enough in stating that they mean finally to leave the Soudan; but going to 'Khartoum would be very much like I a recthvguest of the country, and the one Might lead to the other. We are now, as it ( seems to us, at the parting of the ways; and if the country will speak out there will be an end, If we do not altogether mistake its voice, of the cry of "On to Khartoum." Once let it be seen that it is not necessary to go to -Khartoum, and it will soon be perceived that it is -not necessary either to construct a railway or to destroy the power of OSMAN DIGNA. If OSMAN DIGNA will keep himself to himself, why should he be destroyed? He is in his own country, fighting against "fearful odds" for the freedom of his race. We have beaten him and his followers in every encounter we have had with them, and so far as pres- tige is concerned we have nothing to lose by leaving them alone. And so with the MARDI ; his troops have never once made a successful stand against British soldiers. We can afford now to leave him severely alone. General GORDON is dead; he died the death of a hero, but as we cannot restore him there is no heroism in going to Khartoum.

THE Northwich Division of Mid-Cheshire, which will have a member of its own after the Redistribution Bill becomes law, is putting itself in order for the work that devolves upon it. Steps have been taken with a view of securing a Conned and Executive that shall be fairly representative of the Liberal party throughout the Division ; and with this object there was a public meeting at Runcorn on Thursday evening, when repre- sentatives were elected for Runcorn and dis- trict Now that the ball has been set rolling, it is to be hoped that it will be kept rollinr ; for .there is much to do before it can be said that the Division is ready for the forthcoming contest. Meetings of the same kind will have to be held in other districts before the Council and the Executive can get thoroughly to work. This will take time, and we cannot but think that the less time is taken and the better it will be for the party. Progress is being made in the House of Commons with the Seats Bill, and there is no reason to anticipate tint it will meet with such wanton obstruction in the House of Lords as delayed the Franchise Bill last year. There is indeed every likelihood that the Bill will become law during the next few months, and it is quite within the range of probability that various legislative difficulties will be got over with a view to the General Election tak- ing place at the latter end of this year rather than the beginning of next. There is much to be said in favour of such a course of action, and, if the leaders on both sides of the House are willing, there can be no ques- tion as to its being carried out. It will not do in such a contingency to be caught nap- ping; it is a case in which delay is dan- gerous. Mr. T. HANDLEY, who occupied the chair, detailed the steps which had been taken prior to that meeting, and said that , Runcorn and the adjoining townships. were I entitled to elect 96 members to the Liberal
I TIT

Council, which would be composed of 288 Liberal representatives for the whole Division. The meeting then proceeded to nominate suitable representatives, and, the way having thus been shown, we trust to hear of similar meetings being held in rapid succOssion in. other sectionif the kiorth- wich' Division:—Last night, as will be seen from proceedings reported in another column, the Liberals of Widnes were engaged in a similar task—selecting tvpresentatives for the Council upon which the duty will de- volve of nominating a candidate for the new Parliamentary Division of Widnes.

THE Widnes Local Board, despite the warning of one of its members, insisted on Tuesday last on "making itself ridiculous," or, as another member put it, on making the Board "the laughing stock of the country." On the motion of Dr. O'KEEFE, it was resolved, in consequence of the prevalence of measles at Runcorn, to request the manu- facturers of Widnes to compel those of their employes who lived in Runcorn, 'either to live in Widnes, or cease to employ them, in order not to endanger the health of the township of Widnes." According to Dr. O'KEEFE, there are about 700 men living on the Runcorn side of the river who work in Widnes, and it is seriously proposed that they shall be discharged if they do not forthwith engage to reside in Widnes. The thing is preposterous, and we venture to say tint there is not a single manufacturer in Widnes who will act upon the proposal. They know their own business too well to do anything so absurd. Why should they be called upon to coerce and boycott in this monstrous fashion? What is the use of a Public Health Act and of Sinitary Officers, if the task of guarding against in- fection is to be delegated to employers of labour? By all means take reasonable pre- cautions against the spread of the disease ; but the proposal of the Widnes Board is un- reasonable- There is a right and a wrong way of going about a thing, and they are taking the wrong way. The chances are that the " flitting " of 700 workmen would be the means of increasing the epidemic rather than checking it. But possibly it might serve a turn in another way. We observe that one member who opposed the proposal Was taunted with having "49 houses ehipty at Widnes." Can it be that there are members on the Local Board who are think- ing more of Widnes property than of Run- corn measles? The manufacturers must be very simple if they can be used as catspaws to pull other people's chesnuts out of the fire. But we give them credit for having sense enough not to burn their fingers in this , particular way. THE Conservatives of Warrington having made a strict party fight of it in the election of an alderman, it is a matter of course with them to struggle on party lines for the seat now vacant in South-West Ward. They were beaten in the aldermanic election, and, we regard it as an augury that they will be. beaten in the election of a Councillor on Monday next. There was an attempt to sing the praises of their candidate, Mr. THOMAS JOLLEY, at a ward meeting held on Wednes- day evening; but from what we can gather there were not many electors present to listen I to the tune. It appears to have been thought that the best thing that could be said of Mr. JOLLEY was that, as a member of the Board of Guardians, he was in favour of the poor in the Workhouse having a glass of beer' on Christmas Day. The Tories must bring the beer in somehow; but what a pity it is they couldn't say he was "standing treat " in this instance. They might then have said and sung—" He is a jolly good fellow ;", but it is no great thing to boast of to say that , he was very much in favour of the poor fel- lows in the Workhouse being treated with beer—at the expense of the ratepayers. It ' is, we do not deny, characteristic of him; for have we not also heard of his being in favour of treating the Schoolmaster at Pad- gate Industrial School to a bay window which cost the ratepayers Sioo ? There are too many people about who are ready to be generous with other people's money, ir.nd this is how the rates come to be increased. Mr. C. S. BURGESS, the Liberal candidate, comes before the electors with distinct pledges as to economy; and, as there is no record . against him suggestive of extravartnce, it can at least be said of him that there is reason to believe that he means what he says. He has , entered into the contest at the special call of the Liberals ?in the Ward, who were deter- mined that the Tories should not, as they ! seemed inclized to do, ride rough-shod over them ; and ithecomes therefore the duty of all Liberals in the Ward to make sacrifices, if need be, of time and trouble in order to secure his return. It is satisfactory to hear that the canvass on his behalf shows a good result; and •there was a most enthusiastic feeling in Iris favour at the meeting held last night in Friar's Green School - ,room. Liberals throughout the town are eagerly watching the contest; and, if the electors of South-West Ward do their duty on Monday, there can be no question that Mr. BURGESS Will be returned to occupy the Liberal seat left vacant "by the conversion of Councillor CROSFIELD into an Alderman.of the borough.

Senvice OF Sowo AT Roetcortw.—ln aid et the funds of Ellesmere-street Free Church, Runcorn, a service of song entitled " Elijah " was rendered in the sacred edifice on Sunday afternoon. The music was capitally rendered by the chapel choir, and Mr F J Norman read the narrative in a very effective manner. The collection realised a good sum, the audience being a large one. LACEY•STREET MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, WID• was.—At the weekly meetii.g on Saturday evening the sub- ject for discussion was "Oaght the Government to prohibit the sale of intoxicating drinks 2" Messrs Brown, Swale, Jenkins, Rowlands, and John Redid argued in the affirma- tive,and Messrs Poulson, Rigby, Taylor, and Neild in the negative. The meeting decided the question in the affirm I- tive. The Rev R Harper presided. NEW RAILWAY AT RENTON Juscriow.—The Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company on Monday opened a double-line branch railway, about eight miles in length, extending ton Platt Bridge. Wigan, to Pennington. near Kenyon Junction. The line passes through a large coal misiug district, and will be used for all mineral traffic for Manchester and the South, thus relieving the Wigan depot, through which it formerly passed. THE RAILWAY RATES AND CHARGES BILL.—It is said that 280 petitions asking that the petitioners may be heard at the bar of the House of Commons, against the Railway I Bills, have been signed, and are in course of presentation. No fewer than 20 Parliamentary agents are at work in con- nection with this important movement. Corporations, chambers of commerce, agricultural associations, and trade societies, appear to be moving throughout the country. DRAT! or ABBJT Burronat.r..—The Right Rev. Richard Placid Burcball, D.D., Abbot of Westminster, died on Satur- day, at St. Mary's Priory, Wootton. He belonged to an old Lancashire Roman Catholic family. In 1854 he was elected President-General of the English Benedictine Congregation, and held that high office for a period of 30 years. During many years he resided at Wootton, and to hid exertions was due the erection of the beautiful church of S. Mary there. CONCERT AT Mourne—Last night week a concert was given in the Wesleyan School.room, Moore. with the object of raising a special fund to complete the purchase of articles for school and chapel use. There was a large and apprecia- tive audience, and the concert was highly successful. The programme was taken part in by Mrs J N Dalton, Miss Maddock, and Miss P Maddock; Messrs P Silcock, A Fairclongh, and J N Dutton. Miss P Maddock ably acted as accompanist. SHOCKING SUICIDE AT DUTVON WORKHOUSE T. J. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at Dutton Workhouse on Tnursday afternoon, touching the death of James Orford, aged 52, a native of Appleton, near Warrington, who c )m- -mated suicide on Tuesday. Mr. H. Linaker, clerk to the Guardians, was present. It appeared that deceised was admitted to the Workhouse, lafirmary in May, 1884, suffer- ing from a disease of the kidney& He suffered great pain, but being a quiet man bore it with great fortitude and pa- tience, and there was nothing in his actions to suggest that he had any suicidal tendencies. On the morning •in ques- tion he was seen to enter the lavatory, and shortly after- wards Robert France, an inmate, entered the pi ice and found the deceased lying in a pool of blood on the floor. He hid a wound three inches long across his throat, the arteries and windpipe being completely severed. Near his side was a I irge clasp knife with which the wound had evi- dently been inflicted. In answer to the coroner, Mr. Jones, the master, replied that there was no rule against the in- mates having a knife in their possession. On Wednesday he searched a man whom bethought would be affected by the suicide' and found five knives upon him,—Evidence was given by Fanny Blake, the nurse' Robert France, and Samuel Leigh,—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased committed suicide whilst temporarily in-
near

sane. PRIMITIVE METHODIST QUARTERLY MEETING.— The meeting of the Warrington and Widnes circuit was held on Saturday at Widnes, when a very large number of represen- tatives were present from different parts of the circuit. The highly respected minister, the Rev J Calvert, was appointed chairman, Mt S Owens secretary, -and Mr J Whitley sheet secretary. It was found that the circuit was in a prosper- oas state, there being a decided improvement within the last eix months both in the CongregationS, Sunday schools, and In meMbership, 210 members being riported to the confer- enc. The Rey J Calvert was invited, and consentel to remain in the circuit. Special revival services were ar- ranged for at each place; and the students of the Manches- ter The•logical Institute were invited to take part in circuit work. The circuit, chapel, and school accounts were re- ceived and passed. Messrs Dodd, Titchett, Draught, and Owens were appointed to audit circuit and missionarybooks. Society's stewards were appointed and Mr .3 Rollinson,Sicn's Cross, was re-appointed circuit steward. Mr 3 Rollinson was appointed a delegate to the district meeting, and Mr .1 Whitley, vice-delegate. The Warrington trustees were allowed to bold tea meetings and a bazaar for fonds for a new chapel daring the coming quarter, and a sale of work is to be held at Sim's Cross for funds for that place of wor- ship. The appointment of officers at the yearly meetings was confirmed, the minister and officials looking hopefully forward to the future. NETHERLIST WA CERWORES : DANGEROUS CONDITION OF TRH ENCIINE.—A special meeting of Widnes Local Board was held at Alford Chambers on Thursday after- noon. Mr E Carey presided, and there were present— Messrs Forster, Wright, Gaskell, Martley, Webster, and Allen (clerk), and Carr (engineer). The business was to consider a recommendation of the Gas and Water Commit- tee that tenders for Cornish valve gearing to replace the existing gearing of the "James Cross" engine at Netherley. be obtained. This engine was obtained several years ago at a cost of between £3OOO and £4OOO, and Mr Forster now said that it was in such a dangerous condition that Mr. Carr, the engineer, had reported that be would not be responsible for what might oCcar. It was necessary that something should be done at once.—Mr Gaskell moved the adoption of the Committee's recommendation. He said the matter in short was simply this, that the gearing of the engine was the patent of Messrs Daglish and was of a sort that was very liable to breakdowns, and the cost in repairs was extremely heavy, in fact between £4O and .£6O per annum, and must of necessity increase. A firm of engineers had been consul- ted and they had also the advice of another gentleman, and they were agreed that the gearing was not safe, and ought to be replaced by Cornish gearing similar to that of the engine at Stochewell. Through defects in the cylinders the charge for oil and fuel was very great fer.the present engine. The Cornish gearing would cost aboat £lOO to £2OO, and the repairs would cost about £lO per annum.—Mr Wright seconded the motion, which was adopted after a few remarks

from Mr Webster. Ltvairroot, ComYrr SEsstorts —At 'these sessions on Tues- day the following sentences were named :—James Robinson, aged 30, &tremor), for stealing, at Warrington, on the 7th February, a snit of clothes, the preperty of John Ward, 18 months insprisonment.—Wm. Hant, aged 30, a clerk, for obtaining by false pretences from Messrs Holbrook, Gas- ket' and'Co., at Widnes, on the 112th March last and other days, was amounting to ES 13e 11d, six months' imprison- ment. —Catherine Walker, aged /8. for stealing a coat, the property of Samuel Almond, at Windle on the 24th Feb- ruary, nine months' imprisonment—Richard Parker, aged 33, a cooper, for stealing a horse and set of cart gears, the property of James Townsend, at Huyten, on the 10th Feb- ruary, six months' imprisonment. —John Fallon, aged 18, a labourer, for unlawfully wounding Richard Singleton, at Warrington, on the 22nd Felamary, 12 months' imprison- ment—The following were .11ealt with on Wednesday:— Michael Fogarty, aged 40, labourer, who had been pre. vioarsly convicted as a rogue and a vagabond, was committed to prison for nine months, with hard labour, for having left his two children chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union —Thomas Prescot (28), striker, and Patrick Simpson (27), bricklayer, were each sentenced to -.six months' imprisonment for having, at Windle, on the 4th instant, stolen one coat, two shawls, a 'vest, and a shirt, the property of John Prescott.— Ellen Craymour, aged '5O, for having unlawfully and maliciously wounded Mina Craymour, at Prescot, on the 10th February, was sentenced to two years' imprisonment with hard labour—John Hopkins, aged 50, watchmaker, for having stolen two watches, the property of George Cam- mack, of which he was the bailee, at Windle, on the 15th October, 1884, was sentenced to nine months' bard labour. —Ellen Doyle, aged 50, indicted for having, at Eccleston, on the sth March, feloniously received a shawl from Thomas Prescot and Patrick Simpson, who were found guilty of having stolen the property, were acquited. MVSICAL SERVICE AT ACINCORN.—A musical service of a somewhat unique description took plans in St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel on Monday evening, when a chorus of about 200 voices, members of various denominational choirs having lent their aid, rendered examples of old Methodist 'hymn tunes. The character of the service and its object— to aid the funds of Camden Sunday school, and of the Run- corn ,circuit generally—brought together a large audience, the .edifice being well filled. Mr. R. N. Davies occupied the chair, and on the platform were the Revs. E. J. Robinson, S. ?Zees, and T. Hackett, Xessrs J. Simpson, T. Norman, H. Randle, S. C. Beckett, and T. Simister. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman referred to his early and hap- py connection with Camden school, and speaking of the service, observed that in their Wesleyan chapels they did I not err on the side of having too much music in their ser- vices. (1-lear, hear.) He, therefore, thought thtt they ought to render that music as effective as possible. He de- precated the practice of reading out the hymns verse by verse, because the spiritual effect of the hymn was marred by the custom, and because there was no necessity for it. The programme was then commenced. The hymns were rendered ;u a highly meritorious manner, and although the service occupied nearly three hears, the interest was main- tained throughout, the melodies, which are now so seldom heard, awakening the pleasant memories of yore in the hearts of many et those present. Special reference must be made to the hymn "Saviour Prince of Israel's race," sang to the tune "Eglon." The first and third verses were given as a solo by Miss Jones, who sang with praiseworthy expression and taste; the remainder of the verses were sung as a quartet, the chorus joining in the concluding lines. Mr. G. S. Haziehurst played the organ with his usual masterly skill.—During the evening short addresses appropriate to the occasion were given by Mr. Simpson and the Rev. S. Meee. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman on the motion of the Rey. T. Hackett, seconded by Mr Randle, and the services of Mr. Hanle- burst and the choir were heartily acknowledged on the pro- position of Mr. T. Normon, seconded by Mr. Simister.—Mr. Haziehurst suitably responded.—Mr. Randle and Mr. Nor- man were also thanked for the labour they had undergone in organising the service, which was pronounced to be most profitab:e and enjoyable. The proceed in4s closed with the benediction. KAY'S COMPOUND, for Coughs and Clads, is equally service- able for horses and cattle. iltd, is lid, and Os 9d.-4dvt.

THE ANN-rum MEETING of the North-Western Associa- tion of Medical Officers of Health was held in llanchester ,yesterday, when Dr. Hime, of Sheffield, was elected presi- dent, and Dr. Gornall, of Warrington, was appointed vice- president. Dm GENERAL ELRMWX,—Yesterdav, something like a definite statement was toads as ti the date of the General Election. The Government have consulted with same of the best authorities on Registration law, and they fiud that 11 the earliest date on which the elections could be contested is the 15th of Nevember. The new bets could not he got out before that date, and it is said that the whole Liberal party is now united upon one object, which is that the ex- istence of the present Government must not be jeopardised in the meantime. THE POORHOUSE, THE GRAVE, AND VICTORY.—The Ash. mere, Illinois, Citizen, United States of America, publishes the I following facts :—Abram Beaver, an Inmate of the Coles Co., ; Illinois, poorhouse, certifies that he suffered several years with the most acute rheumatism, so that he cmid not labour, and finally became so poor and prostrate he was sent to the poor- house. The physicians gave him up a-id said he must die, but as a lest chaucte they tried St. Jacobs Ott. A. few applications gave rrlief, and by its continued use he Ws9 enabled ts leave his bed. FOOTRACE AT APPLETON, WIDNES.—On Saturday after- noon, a footrace was run, at the Mill-field greunds,Appleton. between J. Carnes and William Clarke. The prize was a silver lever watch, and the distance run was half a mile. There were present about 200 spectators, who watched the race with interest. Carnes led off with a lead of about six yards, and kept it up for 200 yards, when Clarke Cam, up to him. Carnes then gave up, and Clarke finishel the race, and wag declared the winner. LACROSSE.— Widnes v. Liverpool (Sezoncl).—This match was played on the ground of the Widnes Club on Saturday, and won by the home team by seven goals to five. Liver dool, however, played one man short. Sides—Wkines: Carey, Forster, Frager, G Halsall, F Halsall. P Helga, L Kilcrose, T Killcross, Sayce, Thorburn, F H Wylde, and Brandret. Liverpool: M Boumphrey, F Morgan, El Morgan, Armour, Patterson, W Jackson, Thompson, Latham, H Foulkes, P Foulkes, and Rooke. PRESENTATION AT BIINCORN.—AR interesting presenta- tion took place at the Mersey Missions to Seamen, Runcorn, on Wednesday evening. Mr George Mort, who has been an earneet worker at the Mission School, is about to take up his abode in Chester, and advantage was taken of the event to show the appreciation in which his character and services were held by his fellow-labourers. On behalf of the Wed- nesda:, evening chase and the Sunday School teachers, Mrs Allen presented him with a handsome writing desk, and the boys of the first class' of which he was the teacher, presented I him, through Mr W Shaw, jun , an elegant album. Mrs Mort was also the recipient of a beautiful work box, which ishe received from the hands of Mr Allen. Great regret at Ithe departure of Mr and Mrs Mort, and many wishes for ' their future welfare, were expressed by the various speakers, Mr W Shaw, the missionary, delivering an address appro- priate to the occasion. Mr and Mrs Mort responded in suit- able term.. Devotional exercises were engaged in. Runcorue STAR-BOVVEETT BUILDING SOCIETIES. A highly successful concert was given in Bethesda School- room, on Ta stay evening, under the auspices of these societies. Mr T C Beckett presiding. There WAS a large audience, and an attractive programm+ opened with an en- joyable rendering of "Some day" by Mr C Pownal I. Miss Poole, of Widnes, sang " Bunch of cowslips "and'- Pim° " ia am Inner which won her the aeserved plaudits of the company, and Miss N Handley contributed in capital style "The reign of the Roses" and " The children's home." She received a hearty encore for the first-mentioned song. A similAr compliment Vide paid to Mr G F S Joule for his rendering of the song "The outpost.' Mr A Fox gave "The friar in orde-s grey," to whlch his voice was well suited, and Mr R Moore "Phoebe dearest" and" Toe Pow- der Monkey," in bo'h of which he was very successful. Mr T Riley provoked roars of laughter by reading a Lanca- shire ske.ch. Miss F Handley ably presided at the piane. The Chairman delivered an address upon the advantages of Starr-B mkett societies, and Mr %V Handley also made a short speech bearing upon the subje t. The appropriations resulted in Miss Ada Timmins, of Raucorn, tr.dog entitled to £2OO, and Mrs Elizabeth P.escot, of Ellesmere Port, to _ . . .

£4OO for 121 years, free of interest. Tun SCALDING FATALITY AT DUNcoRN.—At the London and North-Western Hotel, Lowlands-road, on Saturday afternoon, Mr T J Ridgway, coroner, held an icquiry into the circumstances connected with the death of John Cross, 28 years of age, who had lived at Surrey-street, Runcorn.— Superintendent Leah and P.S. Walley were present on be- half of the police, and Messrs J 11 S.lkeld and S Pope watched the proceedings in the interest of Messrs Hazle- burst and Son.—The deceased died on Thursday. last week, from scalds rece:vel at Camden Works on the 17.. h ult by falling into a well of saline Heiner at a temperature of 160 degrees fahrenheit. The deceased had informed his wife, Eliza Cross, that he bad been going to the well to put the lid on, when the steam b Aided him and he walked in.— Henry Coleman of 7, Fryer-street, who was employed at the same work as the deceased, depeucl that Cross told hira 'hat he had lifted up the 11l Co the well to ascertaio hew ,G;ch liquor there eas in, sud /h4R went away to sop !Mlle l'q ler Irunning into the pin. In returnhog his foot turned and he stumbled jet.) the well. The ceders of the firm were that the lid must always be kept down. The well was in a room ased by no other men than those in charge of the process, so that no guard was needed besides the protection afforded by the lid itself.—Joseph Both described how he received Cross from the well, and Dr McDougall stated he attended 'deceased, up to the time of his death. He wag severely scalded up to the thighs, and had suffered great pain. Lock- jaw was the cause of death consequent upon the injuries re- ceived on the 17th ult.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental deeth." SALE OF WORK AT WIDIES —With the object of reduc- ing the debt upon Mali's Temperance Hall, Sitnaila Cross, a sale of work took place on Thursday. The building was erected last yeer by the members of the Hope of Appleton (No. 439) I 0.G.T., at a cost of £326, including heating apparatus, and was opened in the autumn by Mr It & Naylor, of Warrington. Towards this sum £ll3 has been raised, mainly by voluntary subscriptions, and by the sale of work it was hoped to still further reduce the debt by £6O. There were four stalls, one containing articles of needlework was in charge of Mrs T Herrison and Miss S Wright. and another of a similar character was presided over by Mrs J Reay area Ms W Remy. The refreshment stall was at- tended to by Mrs Thompson, Mrs Lomax, Mrs Smart, Mrs Broceley, Miss Amite Thompson, Miss Evane, and Miss Denson. The "gentlemen's stall" was under the control of Messrs J Beta, W Smart, and H Beasley. There was alse a Christmes tree laden with toys, B:c., Mrs Hardacre acting as the dispenser of the "fruit." Miss JB SP Morewood and Miss B Hol- lins aided in the sale. A large portion of the articles of needlework were the product of a sewing class composed of the sisters of the lodge, who had laboured with constant zeal for the weltare of the cause. The whole of the arrange- ments were catried out by a committee of which Mr J Thompson was the hots. sec. There was a moderate audi- ence present to witness the opening ceremony, which was commenced by the singing of a temperance melody. The Rev It Yeatman offered up a short prayer, and then Mr J Thompson, who conducted the proceedings, delivered a short , address. A POVERTY STRICKEN HONE AT RIINCORN.—A. THREE DAYS' Fs.—On Saturday afternoon Mr T J Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at the L. da N.-W. Hotel, Runcorn, touching the deaths of Lois Newton. 3 years of age, daughter of Thomas Newton, deck labourer, of Cholmoncleley-place. It appeared that some time ago the child suffered from measles, and medicine obtained from Mr Speakman, chemist, was administered. The child apparently got quite well, but on Thursday she complaincd of feeling very sleepy, and the 'nether noticing Hitt her eyes " looked queer," took her to 'Dr McDougall's surgery. The doctor was out at the tine, bat on his return he found that the child was deart—The Coroner observed that the body ef the child was not in the condition it ought to be considering the age of the chart and be questioned the mother about ter habits and her treatment of the child. She admitted that she was in the habit of taking drink, bat stated that she took every care of her children. Her husband had been out of work for a long time, and for three days last week she had never broken her fast; but she bad always contrived that the wants of the children should be supplied. She knew she could have medical attendance by applying to the relieving officer.— Dr McDougall deposed that the body of the child was fairly nourished and fairly clean. In his opinion death was caused by a fie—The Coroner said the labouring classes as a rule took very great care of their offspring, but there appeared to have been some neglect in this instance.—The jury re- turned a verdict of " natural causes," and expressed the opinion that the mother hal been guilty of carelessness.— The woman was called into the room end the coroner cen- sured her, remarking that had she taken the child to a doc- tor during its illness it might have ben living then. A doctor was provided for the poor, and she could have his aervices for the asking. Many poor people thoreeht if they could get a doctor in at the last minute they could avoid an inquest, 'Moil we, the thine they'feered, but such cases would he merle the subject of searching inquiry. He cau- tioned her to be more careful in future. Lisa ass ORatiNissriote AT Roe:roomer Tnurs lay even- ing a meeting of Liberals was held in dethesde Schoolroom, Runcorn, for the purpose of selecting representatives for the townships of Runcorn, Weston, Helton, Suttee, Norton, Clifton, Bentham, Aston Grange. and Aston.bv-sutton, to a Liberal Cmecil now being formed for the Northwich constituency, acd to reconstitute the orgauiaition in the above townships in accordance with the extension of the franchise. lkir T Handley was voted to the chair, and amongst those present were the Revs S Mees, J D Thomas, W Vause • Messrs J Handley, JP., B Kniveton, W Hand- ley. J R Ftrth, T Norman, F J Norman, P Speakman, W ti Linker, J Bridgewa•er, W Marsh, G Bellamy, J D Jones. W Stanwav, T Whinyateei , S Taylor, G Moss J W Littler, J Knowles, G Millington, and 0 Leak.—The Chairman explaned that Runcorn and neighbourhood were aow included in the Northwich division. At a meeting of the representatives of Northwich, Winsford, Middlewich, and the surrounding districts, held at Runcorn about ten days ago, it was decided to form a fresh association for the new constituency upon the lines of a circular issued by the Chairmen of the East, West, and Mid-Cheshire divisions of the old associations, and that was that the council for the new divieion should consist of one representative for every 200 of the inhabitants. The whole council of the division would number 288. Of this number Runcorn would elect 74. Weston 8, Halton 7, Aston Grange, and Alton-by-Sutton 2. Clifton 1, Norton 2, Stockham and Sutton 2. A meeting of the general council would he held at Northwich on the 21st. In reply to Mr. Speakmet, the Chairman said the Principal business at that meeting would be to form an association for the constituency and to select a candidate.— Mr J Headley, J.P., said seeing that Runcorn had. one- third of the entire representation it was most important that all the delegates shoald b 3 present at the meeting.—Mr. Leak read a eircular which stated that the business of the council would be to consider and decide upon the selection Of a Liberal candidate, to form and establish a Liberal Registration Association, to frame and pass new rules for such association, to appoint an executive committee to act in all Parliamentary registration matters, and to appoint a president of the association and other officers, and for general business.—Mr B Shaw, president of the Runcorn Liberal Association, arrived and took the chair. After some discussion the meeting elected 96 representatives to the council, and it was decided that they should meet in Bethesda Schoolroom on Wednesday evening next to dis- cuss the course to be adopted by them at the meeting at Northwich, and if possible to secure united action thereat. The representatives were also empowered to deal with the work of reorganisation, which the Chairman pointed out should be upon as broad a basis as possible. Ha also re- marked that up to the present the Liberals of Runcorn had the best orgataintion in Mid-Cheshire.--A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings. LIBERAL ORGANISATION AT WIDNES. Last night, a meeting of the Liberals of Widnes was held at Lacey-street schoolroom for the purpose of electing members to serve on a Provisional Committee to frame a scheme of organisation for the consideration of the Liberal party in the new Parliamentary division of Widnes. There was a moderate attendance, and Ms E Carey occupied the chair. Amongst those present were Dr O'Kaeffe, Cap. lain II Brunner,Messrs S K Muspratt, D Forster,J Morrison, D Wright, F Lawrinson, F U Pankhnrst, J W Ware, T Hunter Cczier, S Owens.

HARTLAND WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—In connection with the re-opening services, the &v. W. Potts, formerly of Widnes circuit, preached two sermons on Sunday. Collec- tions were made in aid of the expenses. BETHESDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. " Capital punishment was the subject discussed by the members , of this class on Wednesday evening, when Mr Jas. Aim- head read a paper advocating its abolition. I THE MAGISTRATES' CLERK'S OFFICE AT WIDNES.— AsaT C Spencely, clerk to the Widnes magistrates, with whom is associated Mr C H Lewin, solicitor, has removed his office from 74, Victoria-road, to St. Paul's buildings, oppoe site the police station. MISSIONS AT WlDNES.—During the past week Mr Mack- San, of Liverpool, has conducted very successful mission services in Victoria-road Chapel, Widnes. There have been good congregations each night, and the results of the miresionary's eff _lts have been encouraging. FIRE ESCAPE FOR WIDNES.—The fire escape recently put. chased by the Local Board has arrived, and will ehortly be tried in public. Local Boerd on Tuesday, asking the employers of labour in the township to ceaaoel the Runcorn men employed by them to reside in Widnes, or to accept the alternative of dimissti, has caused considerable excitement. The action is considered as a most unjust attempt to interfere with personal liberty, and the greatest confidence is expressed that the meaufacturers will reject the propesal. The prisoner said his wife bought a sweeping Louth from a hawker, he acknowledged taking some laces, and the hammer he took home to fasten some window blinds, and forgot to return it.—Mr Thomas Winton, manager of the works, deposed that the prisoner had no right to take the articles. Prisoner had been in the service of Messrs Sullivan for five years.—The Bench fined the prisoner 40e, er tonnth's hard labour. ASSAULTING A BLIND WIFE AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions. on Monday, William Shaw, stonemason, Cooper-street, was brought tip under a warrant charged with assaulting his wife, Priscella. The woman, who is blind, stated that on Thursday she and her husband, who had not lived comfortably together for the past few moathe, agreed to seearat ,e sell the furniture, and divide the money thus obtained. Mr Point bought the furniture, but as she would want a home for herself and little boy she purc'eased a few of the things back. She stayed in the bones until dark on Friday" night, when her husband entered, dragged her into the street by the hair, and struck her on the left eye. Nobody dare attempt to get her back into the house, beetle managed to re-enter on Saturday at noon. She asked the Bench to grant her a separation order.—lnspector Roche informed the magistrates that he saw the woman bleeding from a wound on the eye.—The prisoner, who pleaded gui.ty, was bound over to keep the peace for six monthee_himself in £lO, and one surety of £5. THE FAILURE OF A W DIMS TIMBER MERCHANT AND BUILDESI.-Ihe public examination of James Walker Car- tile, timber merchant and builder and contractor, of Widnes, was opened on Thursday at the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, before Mr Registrar Bellringer. The debtor was re- presented by Mr Morrison Draper. The Official Receiver in Bankruptcy, Mr E Gittens, said he could not go on with the examination as no statement of affairs had yet been filed. The receiving order was made on the 28th February, but an extension of time—six days—was applied for aad granted. That time had now expired, and the statement was not filed.—Mr Draper said he would be obliged to apply for a further extension of time. He had an affidavit from Mr Eschelby, who was appointed to assist the debtor in prepar- ing his statement. —The Registrar : What was the debtor? —Mr Morrison: A timber merchant and building con- tractor—The Registrar : What are his liabilities ?—The Debtor: About £20,000, secured and unsecured.—The Registrar (after reading the affidavit) said it appeared from it that a farther extension of time would be necessary.—Mr Draper : I ask for ten days.—The Registrar : Surely the statement can be prepared in a less time if the debtor's books are at all in a satisfactory condition. However, I will grant you a week from to-day on condition that you furnish the Official Receiver with a list of the creditors, and their estimated claims, within two days.—The Debtor : The Court can have a list of the creditors at any time.—The examination was then adjourned for a fortnight.

The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said although the Widnes division as recommended by the Boundary Commissioners had not yet received the approval of Par- liament, there was no doubt such would be the case. unless some very strong reasons were brought forward for a contrary course. At all events, if th=.re was any alteration in the scheme it would be small, and the scheme would not be prejudiced be' their proceedings that night. He explained that at the invitation of Mr E K Muspratt, pretident of the Widnes Liberal Association, the chairmen and secretaries of the various associations in the division met at the Liver. pool Reform Club, and discussed as to what would be the best way to obtain the views of the Liberals of the consti- tuency as to the future organisation of the party. It was agreed that a provisional committee of 27 members should be appointed to draw up a scheme, each township sending& representative for every 2,000 of population on the census of 1881. Widnes would be entitled to 13 members on this committee, which would meet at the Liverpool Reform Club on Wednesday afternoon next. _ . . . _

Mr J Morrison moved that the following gentlemen be appointed : Messrs E K Muspratt, F Pankhurst, Carey, T Snaps, J L Muspratt, F U Gossage, David Wright,. W Wareing, Francis Heyes, John Taylor, II Brunner, J Morrison, and Dr O'Keeffe.

The Chairman observed that Mr R Shaw, a gentleman who had great experience in organisation matters, was un- fortunately unable to serve on the Committee.—Mr P. D Williams said be did not see on the list the name of any man who had earned his bread by the laoeur of his hands, and the sweat of his brow. The gentlemen proposed were all bosses, manufacturers, and grocers.—Mr Forster said the speaker was at perfect liberty to propose anyone he chose.—The Chairman: I don't think there It any distinction between any of us. I thought we were all working-men—doing work as well as we can for oar living Mr Williams : If you had only one representative of the working classes on the committee it would do a great deal mere good for the Liberal party than t) get a clannish lot of people together to represent one another in high Places. (Applause.) Mr. Williams declined to have his name sub. mitted, adding that be simply did not like 'to see any "Clannish " work.—The Chairman said there was nothing farther from their intention tban to do anything in a clan- nish manner.—Mr Williams said he was himself a working. man and knew what working-men said —Mr. Hunter said be was glad Mr. Williams had made the remarks he had, because it was the working-men of Widnes who would have to return the member of Parliament.— Several names were then proposed, amongst them being the name of Mr. Williams.—lt was decided to make the selec- tion by ballot, and Mr. Whitby and Mr. Hunter were ap- pointed scrutineers. The result was as follows :—Messrs E K Muspratt, F H Pankhurst, E Carey, T Snaps, F H Gossage, David Wright, John Taylor, Dr O'Keeffe, H Brunner, J Morrison, P Hayes, J W Waring, and F Law- rime.

The Chairman said there was an effort being made to obtain an alteration in the scheme proposed by the Cam. miseioners by the substitution of Wavertree for Huyton, Hobv, and Whiston. He pointed out that as at present pro. wised he constituency contained about the right number of population—about 52,000 or 53,000. The population was, however, rapidly increasing, and so was that of Wavertree, and if that town was added to the Widnes constituency the division would be much too large, and very expensive and , troublesome to manage. There was not either any C 39. Inanity of interest with Widnes district. He, therefore, moved that a petition be signed by the 'President of the Association, and forwarded to Parliament in support of the Commissioners' scheme.
_ The meeting then concluded with the usual votes of thanks.

THE BOYCOTTING OF THE BOARD. The following Is from a correspondent who has neglected the usual rule to send his name and address • but we print his jeu d'esprit, thinking that, while it is address; but Is at least diverting: There once was an LL.D., An editor, too, was he, Who In things political And evangelistical, Was as neutral as neutral could be. • There, too, was a Local Board, And this editor said, not a word Would he ever report, Either lengthy or short, Of their doings—how very absurd! And what had this Local Board done— This Board that henceforth he would shun? They merely had sent One advertisement To a rival. Now wasn't it fun To see how this great LL.D. Could thus show his" neutralitee," When he'd either "boycott," Or soft soap the whole lot, • By his nice "standing rule "—£ s. d.

It was also in poor condition. At the time the animal was yoked to a cart laden with atraw.—Bradbury was fined lOs and costs, and the servant was ordered to pay costs.

Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, who bad been on a visit to the Queen, returned to London on Thursday morning. Mr. James Lowther has been adopted as the Conser- vative candidate for the South Diviaion of Lincolnshire. Mr Thomas Russell (Liberal) was elected without oppo- sition for Glasgow on Wednesday, in the roomof Mr Geo. Anderson, appointed deputy master of the Melbourne Mint At A meeting held at the Young Men's Christian Asso- dition, Manchester, on Wednesday evening, it was decided to form a temperance political organisation for Manchester, -Salford, and South-East Lancashire. At the Nantwich Workhouse, no fewer than 16 paupers wore attacked with typhoid fever. There are five in the house at the present moment under treatment. There are also two cases of scarlet fever. Mr. Moon, chairman of the London and North-Western Railway Company, speaking at a special meeting of the company on Thursday said the railway companies had no intntion ot abandoning their Rates Bills, as had teen stated.

ANOTHER LONDoN• MysysnY.--Charlas Blake was en- gaged on Monday night at the grating in Lordship-road, stoke Newington, London, when he found the body of a little girl, aged about four. The body, fully dressed, had 'apparently been in the water a few hours, and from marks Upon it violence is considered certain. At the annual meeting ot the Sea Fisheries Protection Association, held in London on Wednesday, great dissatis- faction was expressed at the differential rates imposed by the railway companies for the carriage of fish, and a reso- lution was passed urging traders to resist the Bills now be- fore Parliament to increase the rates. Mr. Noel, M.P., at a meeting of the Artisans' Dwellings CoPanY, on Wednesday, said the Board of Trade was do- ing all that was possible to obtain facilities from the rail- ways for working-men living in the country, and the Great Northern was preparing a scheme for this object. Third- class season tickets available at all hours of the day-were wan!..ed.

MunnErtlii LoNDow.—The Coronet's inquiry in refer- ence to the death of the man Wheaton, who was shot by a fellow lodger named Rose in a house In Camden-road, London, a week ago, has resulted in the committal of the latter for murder. The deceased man had expressed the opinion that Rose shot him through jealousy. It has been ascertained that the murderer has been an inmate of lunatic asylums.

BY SOLOMON SMITHEYS. CLEEANIN' UP. "Cleanliness is akin to Godliness," is an owd sayin Ipossesiin' abeawt th' average ameawnt o' exactness 'at is to 'I,. rec.., oint anyina'. Dai. clew:aloe:es en cleeanin' up,' are not synonymous, an' if cleanliness is akin to Godliness, olteattin' up isn't akin to good-natne or if it is, its a very distant relation, an' many a mon would swop some of his wife's whim for tnrnin' th' heawse topsy-turvey, for some of hl3 neighbour's wife's knack o' promotin' domestic comfort, —if he knew heaw. An' he couldn't be blamed for dama- gin' number ten i' th' decalogue so mitch noather. Some women are never earved if they're not sloppin' an' moppia' an' kickin' up a dust. When they're kickin' up a dust they Ca' it " an' it meeans raisin' a smudge at a November fog's a fop' to. Scientific folk hosed 'at theer's aw scents o' nee-farions lumber i' dust. Fayver germs an' sporads ; microbes an' monads; bacteria an' fronteria; mfasoria an' easel-f °Boris an' th' heckey knows what be- side; but if a mon's tired o' wantin' t' live a bit lunger, let him drop in on a clustin' do an' he con get smoor't reel off. Th 9 principle o' th' thing appears t' be to raise a peck o' dust for th' sake o' gettin' rid of a twoththe tay-spoonfnle ; t' send it flyin' o'er everythin' an' after'rds to wipe it off spots 'at are conspicuous, leeavin' it lyin' i' other places thick enoof to grew sallit in. To say naught o' rousin' up these microscopic monsters afore-mentiont, an' makin' um mad enocf for any mischief. Matty o' Mahogany's ca's thi3 soart o' tidyin'—`4 pasty Dolly wark." " Th' firrups tak' eich wark for me " hoo re- marked one day, "a paa'cel o' slop-pin', slovenly, slummo- kin', slatternly snicketts—an" be far' to tun, if they ea' that cleeinin'." A forcible speyker is owd Matty, an' given to savin' what comes uppermost. Its th' nattle-temper't woman, heaw-ever, 'at's th' cham- pion scrubber an' tidyer-up ; for a woman 'ate too lazy to be heawsepreawd is generally too lazy t' get into a tantarum, of any consequence. Th' best show boo con make o' bad tem- per is a bit of a sulk 'at harts nobody, or a cryin' fit, an' hoo'll not cry if hoo con manage, for then hoo has to wash her face. Ac lung as theer's an even tint on it hoo ne'er heeds, but when it's bin channelled wi' tears hoo has to con- form to poppylar opinion an' sooap an' wayter. But vit a sharp tempte't nit, cleeanin' acts as a safety- valve an' when th' steeam's up, an' th' husban's noan hondy hoo blows off in an aw-reawnd grand scrabbin9 an' tidyin'-up do; an' when th' seawnds o' moposteyls an' broom-hondles clatterin', an' o' pots an' pons bein' dumped down, are "heard in the land," it's safe to surmise 'at theer's a hood to bond tussle gooin' on between a 8t o' illtemper an' a fit o' tidyin'- np, an' at th' missus o' th' heawse is th' maister o' th' situa- tion—pro tem. If theer war not this eawt-let forsome women, the'yd brast; or come to some want end. Theer'd be moor barloed yeded husban's for one thing; to say naught o' faytherless brats an' snipe-nosed widows. A sperrit o' jealousy very often brings on th' cleeanin'-fit state o' mind, an' some women con be jealous of aught, fro' their husban's' constancy to their next dur neighbour's new cap. If a mon wi' this wart of a wife wishes t' be decorated wi' th' order o' th' "Grey Mare" i'th' shape of a big Saint Andro's cross o' stickin' plaister, he nobbut needs to hint heaw tidy some other mon's wife keeps her childer ; or what a good cook boo is; or heaw sweet temper% hoo looks—he'll get knighted uppo' th' spot wi' whatever is hondy an' heavy enoof. But this is a digression, as th' schoo'-maister said when he stopt canin' his pupils to tak' a pinch o' snuff; still, it may be fur' remarked that a woman had better tak' th' mop3teyl to its legitimate use than to her husban's yed ; an' If he's wise, he'll foster th' former idea. Neaw th' sperrit o' emulation is so very nearly allied to jealousy 'at their effects an' results may be classed egether. It's a weel-known fact i' Neeral History 'at one cock 'li set aw th' cocks crovvin' for miles reawnd, an' at dogs 'll vocalize on th' same principle. Women act uppo' this plan 1' respect to cleeanin', an' if one mop's seen trundlin', a whole fowt 'll be agate i' less than ten minutes, an' aught 'at wears breeches taks warnin' an' shifts. Weather's no obstacle. If theer's an Aasterly wind blowin' keen enoof t' nip th' nose off a kest-eighron din-knocker, th' typical cleeaver seems t' tak' it as a godsend, an' hooll be deawn on her knees at th' front step, hearth-stonin,' scrubbin', an: touching' up to that degree, 'at one 'd think hoo're expactin' th' lord a' th' manor comm n' to a state baggin'. Or if it's snowin' or rejoin' an' th' fowt's aw of a puddle, hoo'll cleean th' heawse floor until folk dar'n't cross it, not even on th' keckley edge o' their clogs, an' there's a w'ary time on't till th' floor gets to a fair average again. A neat an' tidy heawse is a thing to admire. Windows at one con see through; a floor 'at one could eat off; fur- niture polished like a lookin' glass, an' th' tins an' th' cro- kery lookin' to breet au' shiny for anybody to hint at their not bein' spotless. An' th' presidia' genius 'll be theer to match wi', as like as not, a pleasant smile on her face, an' , a look o' pride an' satisfaction in her belongins as weel, an' very excusable too, considerin' heaw admirable it aw is. But a heawse o' this kind isn't kept up to th' mark by jealousy or ill-temper. It's done on seaund cleeanin' prin- ciples. By a knowledge o' th' subject 'ate partly due to early trainin' an' partly to instinct—an' which is also as different to owd Mally's "Dusty Dolly work" as Sarah Musselfoot's doincin' is to Madame Taglioni's.—Front Ben.
