THE SOITDAN ADDRESS TO THE TROOPS. DEFIANCE FRONT OSMAN, Koren, Fainex,—Lord Wolseley has issued, a special general order tcathO soldiers and-sailers sihill'have taken part in the Nile Expedition. < It stated that the Qaeen had watched with deepost interest the brave doings of her soldiers and sailors in the Soudan, and desired to express her admiration at the menner in which they had undergone the hardships of the campaTgo. It was Lord Wolseley declared, his highest pride to have commanded sneh a body ot men, and he hoped to lead the force to Khirtonm and to capture that city before the present year was ended. On the river and in the deserrthe army had borne great hard- ships without a murmur, and in their engagements with the 'enemy the British soldiers had been invariably victorious. Khartoum haying fallen through treachery, and the force at his (General Walbeley's) disposal not having been nen- stituted with a view to besiege that place when strongly held by a hostile force, they mast be content for the pre- sent to remain at the be idquarters on the Nile, and to be engaged in preparation for an advance in the autumn. THE JOURNEY FROM GADUL. Memo, FRIDAY Evalcuta.—Lieut. Douglas and a detach- ment of the 19th Hussars arrived here last night. They walked from GAN!, a distance of 93 miles, in consequence of having loSt their hors :s daring the cimpaign in the desert The detachment lost over forty horses, either by being killed or having died from exhaustion in the expedi- tion to Metarnmeh. The remainder of the force which was left behind at Gakdul Is also returning here, but their pro- gress will be very slow. They are also proceeding on foot in consequence of the deficiency of the transport service. The weather is b.coming excessively hot, and the effect upon cur troops is, to say the least, very alarming KORTI, SITNDA.Y.—The Naval Brigade. the Southern Divi- sion of the Artillery, and the Heavy Camel Corps detach- ment have arrived here from Gakdul. They report that the Mandi's scores are approaching that place, probably for the purpose of looking for wood. The remainder of the force from Gakdul is expected to arrive here next week. General Brackenbury, with the Staffordshire Regiment, the Gordon Highlanders, and the Engineets, has arrived from Merawi. All the wounded belonging to the Nile column, includin; Colonel A. G. Wauchope, Captain Horsbrugh, and Lieu- tenants Kennedy and Coulbourne, are doing well. General Brackenbury reports that the natives along the banks ap- plied his men freely with fresh food as they advanced down the Nile. It is persistently rumoured by the natives that the Mandi has instructed his Emirs to prevent the tribes from harassing the British troops. He declares, they say, that be must eventually be victorious, and that the sari will finish his battle for him. The Modir of Dotiaola has loft for Merawl, and All Bey takes command of the Egyptian troops. flown, Moerner. Lord Wolseley to-day inepected the Naval Brigade. He praised the conduct of Lord Charles Beresford and his men, and called out of the ranks the en- gineer who repaired the boiler of the steamer which was sent to rescue Sir Charles Wilson and his party on their way down from Khartoum. He complimented the man warmly, and gave him his own cigarette case as a personal memento. The General afterwards heartily thanked Major Denison and his Canadian boatmen for their plucky, unflinching, and gallant behaviour in the whalers. THE TROOPS OF THE MAHDI. KORTI, TUESDAY Moesusto.—The Mandi, after paying a visit to the tomb of his father at Kirririe, has gone to Abhab Islam, which is situated 130 miles higher up the Nile. He is greatly in fear of death by treachery, and has doubled his personal guard. News, which is believed to be reli- able, has been received to the effect that the people of Khordofan are rising against the Emir, who is the Matsdi'is uncle. It is stated that the barges ordered by Lord Wolseley, for use on the Nile for the conveyance Of stores in the first instance from Assouan to Dongola and Korti, and subse- quently as store boats in the autumn campaign, are being built by Messrs Samuda 8r05.,. at the lee of Dogs. They will be towed by steamers which are about to be built by contract. Lord Wolseley's eyesight has not as has been stated in any way been affected, and the state of his health is in every respect satisfactory. He has only one eye, having lost the other in the Crimea. The Government have made extensive purchases of iron rails similar to Hawse used on the Government Railways in India. These rails, which are being made at Middlesbor- ough, are to be laid on a gauge of 3ft Gin along the Nile where Lord Wolseley may direct. Two engines have like- wise been purchased for use on this railway. Woolwich Arsenal is to turn out the immense number of 2,500,000 cartridges a week from the present time. Iron tanks to hold 14 gallons of water, to be along pannier- wise, are being made as rapidly as possible, and also all kinds of wooden boxes. A detachment of 15 trained telegraphists of the Royal Engineers Reserve of the Post-office Volunteer Regiment, who are about to proceed to the Soudan, were on Monday addressed by Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, the Postmaster-General, at the General Post-office, prior to their departure for Alder- INSPECTION BY LORD WOLSELEY. KORTI, WEDNESDAY MORNING.---Early this morning Lord Wolseley inspected the Heavy and Light division of the Camel Corps. Notwithstanding the hardships they have undergone the troopers presented a splendid appearance, and were warmly complimented thereon by the General, who also thanked them heartily for the excellent services they had rendered. Immediately after the inspection the Heavies started in boats for their new camp, near Abu Fatmeh, where they are to spend the summer. General Brackenbury started north this morning. He is also travelling by the river.

THE RETURN FROM GAKDUL. • KORTI, WERNESDAL—Foeir companies of the Royal Irish Regiment have arrived from Gakdul. The last detachment of the desert force is expected to reach here on Saturday next, Colonel Wolseley, commandant of the Heavies, and one company of the Royal SUBS2X Regiment, have left in whalers, the former for Abu Fatmeti, the latter for Abu Gusi. The steimer Lotus, with a nuggar in tow containing the four wounded officers. Colonel Wauchope, and Captains Kennedy, Walsh, and Beanett, and 36 men of General Brackenbury's column, left this evening. Lord Wolseley in- spected the Guards this morning preparatory to proceeding to his new head-quarters at Dongola. THE SUAKIM EXPEDITION. CAIRO, SATURDAY.—The Yorkshire Ragiment, instead of being sent to Suakim as originally intended, will pro- ceed to Aasouan, to replace the Egyptian Infantry ordered from that place to Sarrue, to assist in the construction of a railway from Sarrus to Akasha, a distance of thirty- eight miles. Toe necessary plant is now on the way from England. CAIRO, MONDAY.—Lieutenant-G[eneral Sir G. Graham left here for Suakim this morning. Stumm, SAVIRDAY.—The Amaras are delighted at the presence here of British troops, and are ready to desert at the right moment. A native woman has just come in from Tamai. She states that there is a scarcity of food there, and the rebels are alarmed at the eight of the ships con- stantly arriving at the harbour. A spy from Hasheen states that the rebels have sent their women and cattle into the mountains. Enemas, StlNDAY.—Three Bedouins belonging to the tribe Amara have arrived in camp this evening. A portion of this tribe are friendly to us ; but another section has joined Osman Digna. and are now in his camp. These Arabs have brought in a letter from Osman Digna to the General commanding the British forces here. Osman begins by recalling the chief events of the Soudan war during the
AND T'

last two years. He recounts the defeat and annihilation of General Hicks, the defeat of Baker Pasha, capture of Sinkat, and refers to the fall of Khartoum, the death of General Gordon, and the retreat Of Wolselev, driven back by the Mandi to Dongola. He -announces that the fall of Kassala is imminent, and that the triumph of the Mandi in the Soudan will then be thorough and complete. He solemnly warns the General not to sally mitside the walls of Suakim, as if he does so his army will be driven into the sea, none being spared save those who will embrace Malabmetanism and become soldiers of the Mahn

SUAKIM, TIIESDAY.—The Indian Government transports Schzada and Hurzara have arrived from Bombay with 400 men and 460 horses of the Indian contingent. The hired transport Australian with General Freemantle and Grena- dier Guards, have also arrived. Three Sikhs were stabbed last night by rebels, two of them being mortally wounded. One rebel was shot dead by a sentry. WHDNESDAY.—The rebels again approached the camp of the Sikhs last night and killed a sentry. They then retired. The Shropshire Regiment has landed. • ATTACK ON THE BRITISH AT SUAKIM.

SUAKIN, TIIIIIISDAY, Q-45 P 31.—Lite1y marand:ng par, ties of the enemy in twos and three have pushed into the camps for the purpose of plunder. Last night these raids as. Sumed more serious proportions. Fifty rebels attacked the Ordnance Corps, killed two men of the Berkshire Regiment who were on guard, and wounded three others. Toe rebels escaped, taking with them six killed and leaving the body of a sheikh.

Another raid was made on the camp of the Shropshire Regiment. Two of the men of that regiment were killed and one dangerously wounded. One is missing. It is not known whether any of the rebels were killed. They escaped owing ts the darkness. • The camps are much scottared, but every precaution has been taken against further attacks. Redoubts and ditches have been mode round all the camps, and the sentries have been trebled. General Graham arrived this evening. He was met be' the Staff. He is much better. The General sleeps on board ship to-night and lands to- MOITOW. THE LOSS OF LIFE IN EGYPT.

A Parliamentary return, applied for by Mr. Stanley Leighton, M.P., was issued on Wednesday, showing the number of cisualties in the army and navy during the English occupation of Egypt from July, 1882, to March, 1884. In the bombardment of Alexandria there were five killed and 27 wounded of the naval contingent; at Kass. seam eleven British soldiers were killed and 108 wounded, four of the naval contingent were killed and 50 wounded, and one of the Indian contingent was killed and four wounded ; at Tel-el-Kebir 61 British soldiers were killed and 317 wounded, 13 of the naval contingent were killed and 63 wounded, two of the Indian contingent were killed and seven wounded ; at El Teb the army lost 30 killed and 129 wounded, and the navy five killed and 26 wounded ; at Tamasi the army lost 94 killed and 91 wounded, and the navy lost 13 killed and 25 wounded •, while from miscel- laneous causes nine soldiers were killed and 32 wounded, five Of the naval contingent were killed and 32 wounded, two of the Indian contingent were killed and four wounded. This gives a total of 225 killed and 915 wounded. In addi- tion 46 soldiers aril 17 sailors and marines died of their wounds. Excluding those killed in battle, 766 soldiers and 96 sailors and marines, and nine of the Indian contingent died in Egypt ; while 3,939 soldiers, 417 sailors and marines, and 49 of the Indian contingent were invalided home from cause other than those of wounds. GENERAL GORDON. A supplementary estimate is for a grant of £20,000 to the family of General Gordon, it being added that this sum will be paid to trustees. and will be applied by them for the benefit of General Gordon's family, in accordance, as far as possible, with his last wishes, in such manner as the Queen may direct. The Times announces that the sixth volume of Gordon's diary has arrived in London together with other papers. The diary is, we are informed, of the highest possible in- terest. It is written upon the backs of Egyptian telegraph forms, and bound together with strong twine. It is fall of illustrations, and in style is highly characterestic. Evi- dently on the 14th of December, when the diary closes, General Gordon had little hope that relief would reach him in time.

The Press Association understands that a portion of the late General Gordon's diary has now reached the War Office, but until the whole of it has been received no deci- sion cart be taken as to how it shall be dealt with. A repre- sentative cf the Press Association had an interview yester- day afternoon with Sir Henry W. Gordon, brother of the late General, who had not then received any intimation ae to the arrival of his brother's diary, nor as to whether it would be published in whole or in part by the authorities. Sir Henry received on Tuesday a letter from the late General Gordon, dated Khartoum, 14th December, but it is of a pri- vate nature, dealing almost entirely with family and dean- cial matters. By the same mail the King of the Belgians and the Misses Gordon, at Southampton, also received let- ters from the hero of Khartoum. It was not in any way at the rrcoest or instance of the family of the late General Gordon that the Government have proposed to them a vote of £20,000. Indeed. it was intimated to the Prime Minis- ter a short time ago that the family were averse to receiv- ing any public grant of money. The late general has, it appears, left a will, but in the absence of direct evidence of his death there is expected to be some difficulty in formally proving it.

CANADA AND TUB DYNAMITEB9.—A bill has been intro- duced in the Dominion Parliament, providing that any person maliciously causing an explosion of dynamite, or manufacturing explosives with intent to destroy life, shall be guilty of a felony punishable by imprisonment for life.

_ EDUCATIONAL Gnstrrs.—A Parliamentary return issued on Saturday states that the annual grants in England and Wales for day scholars came to £2,770,855, showing an in- crease of £260,234. Church of England schools received £1,418,242 ; British, undenominational, and other schools, £237,112; Wesleyan schools, £120,807 ; Roman Catholic schcols, £150,394; and Board schools, £987,918. ATTEMPT TO UPSET A RAILWAY TRAIN.—On Saturday night an attempt was made near Arbroath to wreck the ex- press train which leaves Dundee for that place at six o'clock. Several woeden sleepers were placed on the line, but fortu- nately the engine, one of the most powerful belonging to the company, was able to cat the sleepers into matchwood. The passengers sustained a severe shaking. The engine kept on the metals. HAndsome rewards have been offered, but nothing has been discovered to lead to the apprehension of the miscreants. FAITH-HEALING MISSION
AT WARRINGTON.

. . . On Tuesday a number of ladiea and gentlemen from Liverpool, .believers in the principles of Faith-leafing, commenced what is called a Betshan mission its Orford-lane chips'. The opening meeting was held in the evening. when an exposition of the subject was given .by Mr. Brig. nail, of Liverpool, to a good congregation. He said that the newspapers in all parts of the country were turning their attention to the subject on which he was • speaking. A.-leiverpool paper of that day devoted a leader to the sub- ject;" endeevonring t 3 shoe, that -because a medical man from London visited Hanley and there witnessed - what was , alleged to.have taken place in the Salvation Army, and that because he did not exectly agree with those who believed in faith-healing, therefore they must be wrong and the doctor right. He might state at the outset that they were In no way Connected with the Salvation Army. ,They would probably fited, if . the question :was asked, that every lady and gentleman on the platform belonged to different religie one bodies, but on the subject of faith-healing light had en- tered their minds. He did not care if the doctor from Lon- don who visited Hanley was present, or if all the cloOtrare ic Warrington were present, they would never be able to over-' throe or disprove the statements that the healed Ones would . be able to give. He held in his hand a small copy of the New Testament, and he believed that book contained suffi- cient proofs fer him to conviace them that the Saviour died that their sins might be forgiven, and that'when He died on the cross He had a twofold object, to cure sin and disease. bid they believe that or only half the Gospel, that the &vim= died that there souls might be saved, but that their bodies might be polluted and diseased ? Ile supposed that there was not a man or woman present so sceptical as not to believe that Jesus rose again after being taken from the Gross. If they took away the fact that our Saviour was a risen Saviour they destroyed the whole Christian religion, but if they believed that He not only rose from the tomb, but ascended into heaven, they were in perfect accord with the basis of their common faith and Christianity. He then read verses 14 to 17 of the 16th chapter of St. Mark. He made no claim to cast out devils, but did claim to be a believer, and that he "spoke with a new tongue" concerning 'netters spiritual. What he wanted to enforce upon their attention was the clause (St. Mark 16c., 18v), "They shall lay hands OQ the sick, and they shall recover." Who was to do that? He thought they had sufficiently followed to see that it was he who believeth should lay hands on the sick. These words were said by the Saviour himself, and what gave them more force, were His last utterance. He could imagine Some saying, "Did you ever see that done, and did you ever see anyone recover?" Some of his friends present would be able to answer that qaestion. Having given other scriptural quotations in favour of his contention. Mr Brignall said that he should in justice to his friends on the platform say that while he knew they were in accord with the general principles that he was teaching, he should not like to say that any of them were prepared to endorse every sentiment that he gave utterance to. He was there to speak his own opinions, and it was sufficient for him if be could disprove any objection that might be urged against divine healing. He heard a statement made the other day in Liverpool by a gentleman from London to the effect that a lady had written from the country to the Bethehan in London asking where she could buy some of the oil for ointment, what kind of oil it was, and if it would cure all diseases. That lady was highly mistaken. The oil was not to be bought and used like a medicine. The oil used in the anointing process was simply pure olive oil, formerly and up to the present. But it was a question as to which there was some doubt whether it was a•berolutely necessary that in order to be healed the application of ointment should be made. He held that it was necessary if they were suffering, and desired through prayer and faith to be saved, that they ehould be anointed with oil. At 161, Islington, Liverpool,. was an institution carried on for the promotion of faith healing, which was doing a great deal of good, and many of therlarge number of persons who had been healed had been anointed with oil. He had seen those who had been anointed with oil who had been suffering from various complaints and diseases for years instantly cared. He had seen an old lady, who from bodily infirmi- ties had been unable to kneel for four years, able to go on her knees and give thanks for her cure. Another case was that of a little boy who had been paralysed since he was eleven months old, who had reached the age of fifteen years, and who was unable to walk and feed himself. He had not been able to see from infancy. By the power of prayer and faith he WAS blessed with partial eight, and before he left the Bethshan was both able to walk and feed himself. No medical man attended him, and it was simply the operation of the power of prayer that cared him. Not a soul in Bethshan or in Liverpool dare assume to say that it was through their instrumentality that the boy was cured. In conclusion. Mr Brignall said that the testimonies that would be given by friends who had attended from Liverpool were incontest- able.—Another lady, who speke with great earnest- ness, then said that she had been fire and a half years a sufferer from heart disease,. had been under five doc- tors, and "there was no soundoese in her." Twelve months ago last October, when almost too weak to speak, she went to the Bethahan, and was healed. "There was no medicine needed," she said, only believe."---A young lady said that for eight years she had suffered from consumption was un- der ten different physicians, no expense was spared on her behalf, but "the great Physician healed her, without money and without orice." Her spinal cord was paralysed, but she had not been in the Bethshan above two days when she was able to walk about like other people.—Another lady testified to having been cured of dyspepsia, after the doctors had said she would never recover.—lt was then announced that the mission would be continued some time, and invitation was given to all suffering from pain and disease to, attend the meetings.

A LION TA-ME-R-Lio-11. RIND By A LIONB9S.—At the Paris Winter Circus, on Sunday, Williams, a lion tamer, was attacked by a lioness, and had a desperate struggle for his life. The audience, while the struggle lasted, was thrown into a state of great excitement. Williams eventually got out of the cage, but immediately fainted from loss of blood. A rush was made to the diors by the spec• tators, who were panic-stricken. Williams' wounds aro very serious. TERRIBLE MURDER IN IRELAND.-.On Monday morning a man named Turley reported to the Newry police that he had been attacked on the roadside by'ssveral men, and that when his wife attempted to protect him, she was kicked and beaten to death. loctairies were made, and resulted in the arrest of Turley on a charge of having himself inflicted the fatal injuries daring a drunken quarrel. A woman's hair was found adhering to Turley's bloodstained clothes. The murder was at first reported as having originated in an agrarian dispute. AN INFERNAL MACHINE AT Cong.—One of these machines was seized at Cork on Saturday in unoccupied premises at Cross's-green, near the Protestant Cathedral. It was found in a chimney, suspended by a rope from a crossbeam, and consisted of a square box twelve inches by nine inches, in two compartments, the smaller of which contained clock- work, the other being filled with about 91bs of blasting powder. Small pieces of iron and a broken bottle were also packed in the case, and about twelve feet of fuse. When placed on its side the clockwork began to tick. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL

An adjourned meeting of this body was held in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presiding. There were also present Aldermen Cromfield, Burgess, Davies, Holmes, Kean, and Webster; Councillors Broadbent, Ashton, Barker, Greening, Francomb, Dixon, Bolton, Burgess, Dakio, Flom- log, Hutchinson, Litton, J. Pierpoint, Mackie Milner, Sut- ten, Taylor, Platt, Tinsley, and Wright ; 'Messrs. Brook (toe n clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), and Longdin (borough surveyor). SANITARY OOMILITTEE.—DISCUSSION ON THE INTERCEPT. ING DEPOTS. The follewieg recommendations of the Sanitary Com- mittee came on for consideration:" That a plot of freehold land off Birchall-street, containing about 3,800 square yards, be purchased from Mr. Wm. Sharp, at 45. 7d. per yara ' • and that a plot of land, containing about 1800 square yards, on the south side of the works belonging to hissers. Roberts., , Dale, and Co., Mersey-street, be leased from Messrs. Roberts, Dale and Co., at 4d. per yard, for the purposes of an inter- cepting depot, in connection with the proposed extensions at Longford, Subject to the approval of the Local Govern- ment Board." -; - In response to a request by Councillor Platt, the Mayor read, after some conversation with the Council and the Town Clerk, two 'memorials respecting the first recommenito: tion in regard to Birchall-street. In one the occupiers of dwelling-houses in the vicinity of the proposed depf:it pro- tested against it being established. The fact of so many vans coming past the doors at meal times, and continually during the day, would be annoying and offeosive, and com- pel them to remove to some other part.of the town. In the other the owners of property in the neighbourhood protested most strongly against the adoption of the site chosen on the- ground that the existence of such station will seriously depreciate the value of property, and reduce the letting ' value. They were of opinion that the 'tenants would re- move elsewhere rather than live near it. • The first memorial was signed by 139 persons,. and 27 persons signed the latter. Alderman BURGESS read a report on the Subject of the. depots, which had been prepared by the Borough Surveyor, who had been in communication with the representatives of Mr. Dutton. The Borough Surveyor stated that in accor- dance with a resolution that he should report upon an alternative site for an intercepting depot for the south side of the borough, he bad considered the sites for intercept- ting depots for the south-east, south-west, and Latchford Nvards. The land the committee recommended the Council to lease was very suitable for a depot, as the whole space could be utilised without waste. The total cost, estimating for covering the brook on the south side of boundary walls, would be about £770. He had inquired about a piece of land belonging to Mena. Dutton's trustees, on the south I side of Howley-lane, with an approach from Napier-street, and on the south . side of the land belonging to Messrs. Roberts, Dale' and Company.. Owing to its position it was. liable to floods, which would necessitate the level of sub-way floor being constructed about 31t. above the present surface of the ground, which would involve longer approach roads and increased oast of banding. He estimated the total costs at £1,400. After remark's had been 'made by Alderman Davies, Councillor Milner, Councillor Bolton, Councillor Mackie, and Alderman Burgess, the Borough Surveyor, in answer to a request made by Councillor BARKER, who thought it, was due to the ' members of the committee that the Borough Surveyor should give them all the inforMation possible on the subject, explained the position, advantages, and disad- vantages of the various sites that had been considered. • Alderman CROSFIELD sa.d that no matter what site was selected there would be cemplaints. The committee belie- ved that Messrs Roberts. Dale, and Co's. site was the least objectionable they, could find, the Borough ServeyOr had given the matter great consideration, and he thought that the Conned .woiald do well to. accept the site proposed. Councillor PLATT then- moved. as an amendment "that the minute having reference to a plot of land off Birchall- street, be eot confirmed." Ile thought that it would-not be right to disparage the memorials received. He thought that it Would be a great hsrclahip on the inhabitants and property owners of any part of the town to have a depot of that character in proximity. It was a fact that for a plot of land in .Birchall-street they were giving 50 per cent mom than- the mileage value of the land, simply because the _vain° of the surrounding land would be de- teriorated. But it was not:open to all the property owners in the neighbourhood to recoup themselves for the lower letting value of their land which would result. If that site were adopted it would inflict a serious blow on the exten- sion of the borough in that neighbourhood. He knew that some gentlemen had fixed upon a piece of land in that neighbourhood for the. establishment of a biscuit factory, but the idea was thrown up immediately, as the two things could net exist side by side. He should also like to ex- press the opinion that they should not ran into all thie ex- penditure until everything was in satisfactory working order at Longford, Councillor BOLTON, who thought it would not be right to place the depot in the midst of increasing cottage property, seconded the amendment. Councillor BURGESS and Councillor MACKIE supported the amendment on the ground that it would be better to try the experiment with one place before adopting a second. Councillor BROADBENT, as a councillor for the North-east Ward, attached great importance to the memoriale, and could not, in the face of them and a deputation of owners and occupiers that waited upon him, support the minutes of the committee in this matter. Councillor Greening, count:liner Sutton, the Mayor, and Alderman Davies, and Alderman Crosfield spoke in favour of the minutes. A vote was then taken, with the result that eight voted for and seventeen against the ameedment, and the minutes of the committee were then carried.

div.head: PAVING OE BRIDGE-STREET.
div.p: THE PAVING OE BRIDGE-STREET.

Alderman Kam; moved the adoption of the minutes ok the Paving and Sewerage Committee, which contained a recommendation that Bridge-street, from Friars' Gate to Rylands-street, be paved with suitable Irish setts. He said that it was thought that suitable Irish setts were preferable to wood, especially in that part of Bridge-street, on account of its gradients. The Borough Surveyor assured thp cora- mittee that Irish setts smoothed for the purpose would be almost noiseless. Councillor TAYLOR seconded the adoption of the minutes. The MAYOR mentioned that a memorial, signed by some of the principal inhabitants of Bridge-street, had been re- ceived petitioning the Council to pave Bridge-street with wood instead of setts. He read this memorial, which we gave last week.
_ Alderman BURGESS : There are principal inhabiants of Bridge-street whose names do not appear on that memo- rial.

The MAYOR: Oh, no doubt. Alderman WEBSTER Some of the principal inhabitants in the upper part of Bridge-street may not have signed. Councillor dome PIERPOINT said that owing to the steep gradient of Bridge-street it must be very dangerous for horse traffic to pave it with wood. Where they had a level piece like that in Sankey-street there was no objection to wood, but even there in frosty weather it required that some sharp material should be sprinkled over it early in the morning. Ile was told by a shopkeeper in Sankey-street that during a recent frost no less than six or eight horses bad been down in one morning. If such were the case in a level place, what would be the result where the gradient was like that in Bridge-street. He thought there would be many accidents, and perhaps some deaths caused. Councillor WRIGHT said the matter had been very care- fully considered by the comeeittee, and under the guidance of their Borough Surveyor they had come to the conclusion that sett pavements were best for Bridge-street, on account of its gradient, and also on account of the cost of mainten- ance. The granite setts they proposed to put down would last 25 years, while wood would last some 10 or 11 years at the most. But what was most serious was the cost of main- tenance. This cost in the case of granite setts would be £67 per annum, and that of the wood setts would be £lB4, and the first cost would also be considerably increased in the case of wood. The MAYOR asked what was the gradient of Bridge-street from Friar's-green to Rylands-street ? He thought it was very small.
The Bouorrau Sr/toreros said the gradient from Market- gate to within about 100 feet of the South side of Rylands- street was one in thirty-two, beyond that it was one in eighty-four.

-Alderman WEBSTER moved that the recommendation with reference to the Irish setts be not agreed to. lie thought that the respective cost of the two kinds of pavements was the very last thing that ought to be considered. What ought to be considered was simply what would conduce to the greatest comfort of those who had to transact their bust- nem, and also what would induce customers to go into shops to transact business. Bridge-street was one of the main streets—or rather, unfortunately, it was once—and they. ought to consider what would bring business back to it. That was not to be done by putting down pavement which would be both noisy and dangerous. They had the ex- perience of other towns to show that wood pavement ceuld be safely utilised in streets whose gradients were as great as these of Bridge-street, and besides if horses fell down on wood they would not hurt themselves, while if they fell on flinty stones the result would be serious. Councillor MACKIE maintained that it would be bettor to leave the paving of Bridge-street over till the improvements had been made there. He seconded the amendment. Councillor PLATT said he would vote for ttle amendment I on the ground that it was better to leave the matter alona for .the present.

Alderman CROSFIELD said be should support the amend- ment. He thought It would be a mistake to pave just a small portion of Bridge•street in the manner proposed when those alterations were going to he made. It was just pos- sible that it might then be decided to pave it with wood. It would be a dangerous thing for anyone to drive over those setts in Bridge-street, and at all events it would be batter to pave the street with only one kind of pavement. • Councillor J. PIERPOINT said his purpose in getting up was to prevent the laying down of wood pavements, not that he had any objection to the thing standimg In abey- ance. He woold therefosa vote for the amendment in order that the matter might remain in abeyance till the improve- ments were made.

- - Alderman BrRGESS. said the condition of that part of Bridge-street was simply disgraceful, and it was not in the Power of a better committee than the present Paying aad Sewerage Committee to keep it in repair. (Laughter.) He thought the present macadam was infinitely more dangerous than sett pavements. He would support the proposals of the committee. If they paved Bridge street with wood bow could they refuse the people in Horeemarket-street.

It has been thus used for more than half a centary, healing the most inveterate diseases, and giving joy and health to vat numbers, The power of the Green Mountain Vegetable Oint- ment is astonishingly great. RUNCORN AND WIDNES. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting WU held. on Tuesday.- Present-- Idessre Carey (chairman), Dr O'Keeffe, Wright, Midwood, _Dutton, Gaskell, Webster, Forster, Pankhurst, Handley, Houghton, Manley. J T Allen (clerk), Carr (gas engineer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspector). THE PROPOSED INCORPOILLTION.—The Clerk, in accor- dance with instructions, had communicated with a number of towns on the subject of incorporation, and he had pre- sented a report in which he said the official expenses seemed so be greater wider a corporation, chiefly caused by greater public improvement being undertaken. AS to the cost of charter, the amount of £220 was only part of the cost, a .great portion of the work was done voluntarily. The large amounts were caused by opposition to the scheme of incor- I poration. With regard to intarest it appeared that in the matter of borrowing very little if any advantage would be de- rived from the change. Under a corporation the Board's books Mon}d be kept in a more satisfactory way. It was impose sihia to say what effect the County Bill would have upon dooal authorities other than corporations; the latter, how- ' ever, would be exempted from its provisions,—Dr O'Kecffe moved that the consideration of the subject should be de- ferred until next monthly meeting —Mr Dutton seconded. --Mr Gaskell sugdested that it would be better to postpone the matter until after the electioo. It was a big thing for the last meeting of the Board to consider.—Mr Webster supported the motion. It was a matter that wanted settling, and in his opinion incorporation would be a benefit to the tows—The motion was carried. THE STOPPAGE OF WEST BANK-STREET. The follow- ing letter was read from Messrs Bolton and SOn We are ;maims to make application to Quarter Sessions for per- mission to close that portion of West Bank-street which di- naVides our works. We eheuld be much obliged if your Board would reconsider the matter with a view to rescind- Aug the resolution which they passed some time ago instruct- ing the Highway Committee to oppose our applications, as we are informed by Mr Robert Davies that we cannot even make the application to sessions until this is done. It ap- pears that when the matter was last brought before the Board the chief opposition was raised by Dr O'Keeffe on behalf of the Roman Catholic schools, and we have since ascertained from Father Claeke that their objectionois not on the ground that any inconvenience would arise through dicing the street, bat on the general ground ot a protest against the development of works in that locality, because ' he considers that they have been badly treated by Hutchin- soo's trustees in having lot ground for manufacturing pur- poses after representations which they made to the school truetees at the time they took the site for school purposes. We think that in common fairness this is a point which should be a matter of arrangement between the school trus- tees and the trustees of Hutchinson's estate and not one for which we and the ratepayers of Widnes should be made to suffer."—Mr Midwood said the Highway Committee had done all they could in this matter, and he did not see that the Board could do any more. He would, however, propose that a deputation consisting of the Highway Committee and Mr Gossage, and Dr O'Keeffe should arrange a friendly meeting between the owners, the ground • landlords, and !dams Bolton and Sens, and all parties interested, and if they could agree upon some common action, he did not see ; that the Board would have anything more to do in the matten—Dr. O'Keeffe, whilst urging the force of Father Clarke's contention, said he would readily fall in with Mr. Midwood's proposition, and he had no doubt that Father _Clarke would not throw any obstacles in the way of de- veloping the trade of Widnes. He would, in fact, do all he could to settle this affair.—Mr. Midweod described how the Hutchinson trustees had endeavoured to get him to take a piece of land in the locality on the ground that no works would be erected near, and that it would bea main thorough- fare, and very glad he was that he did not take it. There ' were 700 children attending the schools there every day, and it must certainly be an intolerable nuisance to be nearly stifled with gas as they were. It was almost inspOs- sih!e for the caretaker to live in the house. He thought Father Clarke's contention a very reasonable one.—Mr. Datton seconded the proposition, which was carried unani- mously. THR Nair Tows Flan : Con OF Anus WasTnn.— Messrs F. and G. Helme, architects of the proposed Public Hall, wrote asking whether there was any particular coat of arms for the town which could be introduced in the space over the archway of the entrance, and if the lettering was'no be "Town Hall" or "Public Offices."—The Chairman thought the panel had better be left blank until they had a design to place upon it, unless they traced a chimney upon it. (Laughter.)—lt was decided that the panel for the preeent remain blank. THE GAS AND WATER COMMITTER —The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee stated that the Broughton Cop- per Company, Limited, and the Liver Alkali Company, Limited, agreed to enter into a contract for water supply for three years on the usual terms. The engineer estimated that the cost of laying the necessary main would be £BOO. It was recommended that the main be laid. During the past month Dr. Campbell Brown had analysed samples of Water from Stockswell and Netherloy. He reported that the Netherley water was " most excellent," and Stockswell witer "excellent," for domestic use. It was decided to offer a reward for information that would lead to the con- viction of persons who damaged gas lamps—Mr. Forster moved, and Mr. Wright seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—ln reply to Mr. Martley, the Clerk said in the Local Act the Board were bound to supply water to a cer- tain area outside Widnes upon a guarantee of ten per cent I on the outlay for three years. These ware the terms upon which the mains would be laid to the firms mentioned in the minutes—The motion was adopted. HIGHWAY MATTERS.—The Highway Committee reported that the surveyor had been instructed to at once erect I "Kent's lamp," and to put a new lamp opposite St Paul's Church, also to remove a lamp in Margaret-street.—The committee, accompanied by Messrs Martley and Houghton, have examined the work (flagging, manholes, dm), com- plained of by W Hodgkinson, and were unanimously of the opinion that the contractor had conformed to the specifics- tion.—Mr Midwood moved and Mr Sadler seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr Wright suggested that the land in front of Warrington-road Board sahool; given to the Board by Mr Gregson, should be fenced.—Mr Midwood pro- , mised that the committee should consider the matter. He ' reported that the diverted footpath at Ditton, and the proposed widening of the road at Crow Wood were still under consideration. Tan HOSPITAL —The Matron had supplied to the Hoe- vital Committee the following list of gifts made to the hoe- witsi during the past year :—Mr H W Deacon, Graphic and • f, Sondea Illustrated News, with Christmas and summer numbers; Mr Whitfield, parcel of "Tit Bits " • Mr Thos "Whitby, " Christian Herald " ; Rev J W Williams, tem- perance periodicals ; Mr Fowler, old papers, dm ; Mrs I Cooper, a scrap book and a number of "Christian" ; Mr • John Shaw, several years' numbers of "Christian Age," " Christian Miscellany," and "Boys Own Paper" ; flowers were given by Mrs James Fallon, Miss Pattison, Mm James 'White, Miss Balmer, Mr C Nickson, Mrs Whitfield, Mrs Jas White, evergreens : Mrs Deacon, Christmas cards, J and E Thompson, "a framed card"; Mr S K Muspratt, parcel of old linen shirts; Widnes Football Club, a conch and two mictures.—Mr Sadler, in moving the adoption of the min- -ides, said there was no doubt these gifts had been of im- ,mense Sane& to the patients, area had served to while away many an hour that would have hung heavily upon the hands of those who;had:the misfortune to be inmates of thelinstatue tion. He was requested by the committee to heartily thank the ladies and gentlemen mentioned for their gifts.—Mr Houghton seconded the motion.—Carried. THE NEW VENTILATING LAMPS.—Mr Carey, in moving the passing of the minutes of the Sewerage Committee, said the burners in these lamps were not arranged as they ought to be, and the surveyor had been instructed to alter them. It was hoped that satisfactory light would then be given. A perfect trial of the consumption of gas by the lamps bad not been made through a nalsunderstanding.—The minutes were passed. THE HEALTH OF THE TOVVE.—THE NIGHTSOILCONTRAC- TOR.—The Medical Officer of Health had reported to the Health Committee that during February there had been 103 , births, or 45 77 per 1,000 of the population, and 27 deaths, I or 120 per 1,000. Eight children under one year, and six between one and five years, had died. One death was caused through zymotic disease. He considered Witt-mad, Victoria-road, John-street, and New-street, Simm's Cross, in a most insanitary condition. During the year there had been successfully vaccinated, 444; died unvaccinated, 54; postponed by medical certificate, 15; cannot be found, 19 ; to ceptible, 0; defaulters, 1; total, being nurnoer of births registered, 533. The committee decided to call the attention of the High. way Committee to the thoroughfares mentioned by the Medical Officer. Mr R Smithson' the nightsoil contractor, Bad asked that £5O (one-half of tha amount deposited with the Board by him) be plot to him as the contract will ter- minate in August. Teo committee recommended that £3O be repaid. lhe Mark It Superintendent reported that the receipts for February amounted to £l5 2s Id, being a de- crease of £2 12e Oel —Dr O'Keeffe moved, and Mr Martley seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr Wright moved an amendment that the minute respecting Mr Smithson be expunged. He deprecated the Board departing from the wool course in such znatters.—Mr Martley said he did not wish going against his own committee's work, but bethought this a bad precedent, and he seconded the amendment.—The Chairman: But you have just seconded the adoption of the minutes. (Laughter.)—Mr Sadler : He will second both of them. (Laughter.)—Mr Martley : It is a little oversight on my part. Perhaps someone else will second the amendment —Mr Webster said Mr Smithson was not a rich man, he hid had some losses of late, and be wanted the money. He thought the committee had always sufficient amount of work in hand to cover the amount, and he sup- ported the recommendation.—Mr Sadler seconded the amendment—Dr O'Keetle said perhaps Mr Webster was not aware that Mr Smithson received five per cent upon his deposit.—Mr Gaskell was of opinion the deposit ought to be withheld until the contract was concluded.—Mr Midwood supported the amendment. He thought the committee had throughout dealt with the contract in a very kind manner indeed, and the Board as business men ought not to return any portion of the deposit until the time had ex- pired.--alr Pankhurst supported the amendment, and Mr Houghton thought if the man was "pinched" the Board -Ought to relieve him to some extent—A member: We are all pinched.—Dr O'Keeffe referred to the low death rate, observing that he thought it was the lowest death rate for the past month of any place in the British Isles. Widnes, although not a very charming place, was, it would seem, by no means an unhealthy place. (Rear, hear.) A Lite . had been secured for an infectious diseases hospital, and as soon as the deeds were signed they would be able to pro- -mod with the buildiug, to that it would be completed before

tensive that it would go round to effect alliances with all coutinet]tal Powers. Stich allianczs have teen effected in the closest manner with the two greatest continental Powera. The Czar is father-in-law to the Queen's second son, whilst wit's respect to Germany—net to mention the various little princelets who have fastened themselves on the fat revenue] of this country—the Emperor and the Queen have grand- phildren in common. Yet it was only the other day that a quarrel with Lteirnany 8( arned imminent, and to-day We are on the verge of war with Russia. It would be pleasant if In reply to those who want t) know what is the practical ass of hinge and Queens, their intermarriages might be cited as pledges of peace. Unfortuswely it cannot be done. Iu the presence of the more acute interest in the attitude of Russia, affAirs in the Soudan have dropped entirely out of public notice. The military operations are confined to withdrawing the troops into summer quarters, though it is intended, if possible, to bring Osman Digna to book as soon es General Graham's force is concentrated. What has hap- pened in the Soudan is almost sufficient to bush the tongues that have so long been clamouring about the abandonment of Gordon. So great is the heat at Korti in this month of March that stringent regulations are enforced to maintain the standard of health. Marching is almost impossible, and the amount of physical exercise is reduced to the minimum. The feared south wind has commenced to blow, and for nearly two months to come will make life a burden to those who are subject to its parching influence. Yet we are still nearly a fortnight off the time at which Khartoum was last year invested, and the first appearance of danger to Gordon as made the signal for the Conservative outcry of rescue. On the 21st March last year there was fighting near Abaf- t:nun ; but Gordon was so strong that be was able to relieve the garrisqn of TialAheh. On the 24th March Khartoum 'lVaa invested.

Now hereabouts lies the crux of thie question of the Mined criminal and cowardly abandonnseat of Gordon by the Government. Supposing that as score as the news of tholnyestment of Khartoum reached London measures were taken to despatch a rescue column, when would it hay& reached the Soudan? This is easy to ascertain from accomplished facts. On the sth of August the Vote of Credit was agreed to in the Commons, and the fore. imme- diately began to move forward. On the 24th •el January, Sir Charles Wilson was acturOy steaming down the Nile en "terctir for Khartoum—say a period of five months from 'lad to finish. Five months from the period when, accord. to the righteous indignation ef political partisanship, the Government should have sent troops to rescue' Gordon, Would have brought the expedition to the Nile in August; that is to'say, at that date such a miserable remnant of a British army as had survived the journey across thrrloodan, desert in dilly would have reached Metemmeh. As 3 hays more than once shown, if the cry were dealt with in another form, and Wire necessary to reply to the charge that Gor- don should have been rescued in the comparatively goo) season of March, it will suffice to eta that, applying the dates involved in the actual expedition,..the rescue colbrem In order to save Gordon in March would have had to' leave England in November, that is two months before Gordon's expedition was dreamed of. These are simple facts. de- monstrable by the simplest examination.of dates, and' yet in spite of them.the cry of abandoning Gordon survives. It is pitiful to. think of the stern silent soldier who saved the Union lying helpless and in incessant pain waiting fer death, the kindest friend that could now visit him. Genera. Grant is dying of one of the most painful and hopeless die- eases that afflicts the human race, and it is aggravated hp peculiar circumstances. Cancer is bad anywhere, but to bredc out at the root of the tongue is to dery the skill of surgeons. There is nothing to do but to suffer, and this G.eneral Grant is doing with the same ohatinate courage with which, just twenty years ago, he sat down before , Riolimond. The latest news describes the addition of in. somnia to his griefs. This is the hardest cat of all. If he could. sleep there would be some temporary surcease o 5 pain. But to lie awake night and day, unable to eat and scarcely able to opeak, goes beyond the tortures of the In.- quisition. Through it all General Grant is- struggling to complete his memoirs. The closing years of his life have. been full of pain and disappointment, and often he must have wished that after the crowning episode of the Appal.. attox Curt House some stray shot had ended-a career thut had just reached a glorious apex. The result of the West Gloucestershire election was no surprise to the Liberal party in London. The Conservative gain justifies Lord Salisbury'sxlesire to take a general dear tion on the present Register. In this instance the defection of Lord Fitzhardinge is credited (or discredited) with the result. But that surely is a baseless imputation upon the independence of the Gloucester electors. The time has I gone by when the leanings of a noblercan, however per- sonally respected, should affect the political fortunes of a great eonstitneney. "The Candidate" is still filling the Criterion, and pro- mises to have an indefinite run. I cloak know what terms Mr. Huntley McCarthy made with Mr. Wyndham, but there is no doubt the latter is coining money. He has already netted over £15,000, and will certainty doable the amount before the play runs out. Mr. Wyndham's usual arrange- ment with successful dramatists who write a play for him is to give them five per cent, on the gross nightly receipts. This makes up a very handsome sum when a piece has any- thing like a long run. But it is doubtful whether such terms were secured by Mr. McCarthy, a young man timidly I proffering his first piece.

The Select Committee of the House of Lords to consider the Manchester Ship canal scheme was appointed on Mon- day. Earl Cowper was appointed chairman, the other members being the Earl of Milltown, the Earl of Arran, Lord Harris, and Lord Romilly. The following bodies have presented petitions to the House of Lords praying to be heard against tber Manchester Ship Canal :—The owners, lessees, and traders in the Wid- nes, Ditton, and St. Helens Diamond Oil Company, andl Hahnemann Stuart, the Corporations of Bootle, Liverpool, and St. Helens, London and North-Western Railway Corn-1 pany, Great Western Railway Company, Shropshire Union Railways and Canal Company. trustees of the River Weaver Navigation, Dean and Chapter of Chester, Salt Charnber of I Commerce of Cheshire and Worcestershire. Mr Thomas Chadwick, Mr R C Naylor, the Marquis of Chohnondeley, Vice Admiral Spratt, Mersey Docks and Harbour Ebard, trustees, of the late John Hutchinson, Messrs Wigg Brothers and Steele and others, the Runcorn Improvement Commis- sioners, Widnes Local Board, and William and Arthur Geo. Guest. TIIR NEW BILL BR/PORE THE LORDS' COSIMITTISR. Oa Thursday the Manchester Ship Canal Bill came before a Select Committee of the House of Lords, this being the third year in succession in which the scheme has been before Parliament. Earl Cowper presided. fliers were 29 petitions against the Bill, 12 of whom were repre- sented by counsel.—Mr. Pember. Q.C., leading counsel for the promoters, in opening the case, said that, in concert with the Corporations of Manchester, Salford, and Warring- ton, the bill was promoted by a body of traders representing a district of Lancashire and Yorkshire, whose commercial importance, if he excepted agriculture was not surpassed in this country, and there was none which at this moment was in greater danger. After two regrettable failures, and , with marvellous pertinacity, this community appealed to Parliament ter the third time to allow them to spend their own money for their own sake, and indirectly for the Dubll .1 good. Having sketched the history of the bills, the learned counsel pointed out that the present scheme dif- fered materially from those of 1833 and 1884. Instead of going through the estuary of the Mersey, the canal from Runcorn would follow the Cheshire shore as far as East. ham Ferry, and there enter the deep water of the Mersey in the Sloyne. The canal could not poseinly injure the estu- ary of the Mersey, and it would be an irretrievable error if it were not sanctioned. It was estimated that the works would cost £7,292,000, which was an increwe of £383,000 , over the estimates of last year, and the increase was due to the fact that the railway diversions were rather more ex- pensive. The share capital was £8,000,000, and the loan capital £2,000,000. He might put down £1,500,000 for the purchase of the Mersey and Irwell navigation, and the Bridgewater Canal, and that would bting the total coat to £8,200,000, and leave a surplus capital of £1,200,000. When the learned council proceeded to speak of the com- mercial advantages of the scheme the Chairman interrupted him, and said that, considering the opinion expressed in that House last year and in the House of Commons in the previous year, the Committee did not think they need go into that matter. Mr Pope, on behalf of the railway com- panies, protested against this view of the Committee, and said be should have to ask their attention to what his clients believed was a wild and impossible scheme. Mr Pember's , opening speech was not concluded when the Committee rose for the day.

Whenever two oe 'three romnymous corres- pondents of a newspaper agree upon a subject calling for public investigation, you may depend upon it there is ground for opening an inquiry. Several writers have agreed on one point—that there is something wrong in the state of the Parish Church ; and in this I cordially agree with them. lam afraid, however, that the public is powerless in the present state of ecclesiastical law to affect any reform. The Rector is just as much an autocrat in appointing his curates I as is the Cam of all the Russia' in taking the lives el the Nihilists. But, though this may be the case, there is one thing that should touch the conseence of the man who, according to Matthew Arnold, should shed " sweetness and light " wherever he goes—l mean the goodwill and respect of his fellows. Can the Rector by any stretch of imagina- tion be said to fall within the great physiologist's defini- tion? I trow not ;on the contrary, he has rendered v
I respect! imagina-

name a by-Word not only among those who were once in his fold, but throughout the town itself. Coming as be did to Warrington with a public recommendation of the highest and most endearing form, he has through a long course of years incurred by his conduct the dislike of his townsmen. So far as the Rector is concerned, a weak and feeble reply has been made by "D," whose special pleading only makes I the case worse. True, the Rector is 80 years old, but are his hopes of immortality to be based upon the restoration of a church, or upon the fact that his bust bas been placed in an art gallery ? Life would be intolerable if these were the only objects to be attained in 80 years of existence. "It is never too late to mend " is a proverb which is gene- rally applicable to humanity, but can it be sad that it applies in the mac of the Rector of Warrington f—Yours respictrully, A DISGUSTED CHURCHMAN.

Sir,—l have been asked to reply to a letter signed-HD,' which appeared in last week's Examiner. and I do so with- out the least particle of ill-feeling towards the Rector of Warrington. Your correspondent says," There are curates and there are curates," but inasmuch as there is always something wrong with the Rector's curmes, ihat remark is irrelevant. For the sake of argument, let it be admitted that the Rector's curates have been a very shaky lot. Then, why on earth, in such an important parish especially, should tbe rector en- gage such men, when he offers, as-he himself has frequently said, as good a stipend as any incumbent in the country? Dots your correspondent " D mean that when the curate come to Warrington they have some kind of a character, but that after a while all the Rector's curates go astray? That is to say that the air of Warrington is vicious. I think I know your correspondent, and if I am not mistaken he has found the town very healthy. I am convinced that your readers will be able very easily to decide whether the Rector merits what has lately been said about him in one of your leading articles. The fact is the Rector has had plenty of good curates willing to labour amongst the dens and courts of his large parish ; but the sin of jealousy is rampant in Church-street, and God's curse , rests upon it, as it did on Saul of old.—Yours respectfully,

[We have bad to strike out a portion of lur correspon- dent's letter, commenting, as it did, unnecessarily, upon events which took place some years ago. We shall give " D " the opportunity of replying en behalf of the Rector, if he thinks fit, and with his letter the correspondence on this phase of tbe question most close.—En. ] A CLERICAL CONTRAST.

Sir,—The Rev, Mr. Tuckwell's lecture on Monday even- ing afforded an example of a wide divergence between men of the same rank and profession. The lecturer displayed the large-minded and la-ge•hearted man who sees the evils of life and feels the generous impulse to lessen them by any and by all the means a good man may employ. Throwing clerical prejudice and intolerance to the winds, he is wil- Hng to adopt any meanr, religious or political, which tend to so desirable a result. Not so his less reverend critic, the Rev. Mr. Carletoa. This gentleman, with an indiscreet zeal not appreciated by his audiencf! rose at the close of the lecture and did hie little best to destroy by ill-delivere cupings the pleasure the lecture had given. When a par- On pad As the iconoclast of pleasant illusions he is on very I treacherous ground. The cobbler should always stick up

for his leather. And one who deals in illusions should not speak ill of them, although they may not have come over his own counter. I fail to see what right Mr. Carleton had , to step, like a black shadow, betwen me and the pleasant illasiOns conjured up by the eloquence of the lecturer. I Doubtless the provocation was great ! For what, to a Tory cleric, could be more galling than the mention of Mr. Gladstone as the originator of the Utopia of I9Bs—with its disestablished chard', its reformed land laws, and its land- lordless land ! So Mr. C., like another irate Tory, arose in his wrath and put his foot into it. He denied that political action would bring about a removal of the evils we are suffering from. Now, I and the majority of Englishmen, think we are even now living in a comparative Utopia when contrasted with the conditions of life in England during the first quarter of the century, when the Toryiem of Mr. C's. type was rampant. And surely this has been brought about by political action, and there can at least be no harm in our striving after further perfection. We may not obtain all we strive for ; but even the strife itself will be beneficial to those who are striking for the right. Mr. Carleton threw cold water over as and our aspirations as a minister of religion, as did the parsecutord of Galileo and the Smith- field burners. In conclusion allow me to say that I shall be glad to hear of the incumbent of Trinity holding an audience as large as that of Mr. 'fackwell's, entranced ad was that by an equally eloquent expooition of the gold to be wrought upon earth when the wori.ers are am, Bac., Penketh, 11th March, 1885. JOHN PEERS. MR. NORMAN AND ECONOMY AT RUNCORN. Sir,—The courteous editorial notice with which 1" Veracity " was favoured in the issue immediately suc- ceeding your publication of "A Aatepayer's " letter, ren- ders ridiculous the supposition with which he opens his reply ; and whether his stupidity was responsible for its being unnoticed, or his scurrility consented to its being ignored, your readers must decide. Acknowledging at once "A Ratan:l9We" mastery of the low invective with whiei he covers. his retreat, I submit that in now suggesting "that the Wvateyan schools are a profit to the denomination'" he admits the complete falsity of hie original insinuation, "that Mr. Merman would benefit by their transfer." With such an admission a manly op- ponent woull eagerly have tendered Bat "amends honor- able" to the gentleman he had malignet ; but "A Bate- paver" contents himself with transferring his unscrupulous accusations to the managers of the school, These gentle- men are as proof against his venom as Mr. Norman, for they make no collection in the chapel, and this statement of "A Ratepayer" is as false as, his assertiim that "after the arrival of the Government grant, the leachers remain unpaid." In Commissioners' affairs. thie censor of public men con- siders an abstract statement from a condensed report euM- cleat foundation for his superstructures, and the weight of his authority may be guaged accordingly. Before rushing into print "A Ratepayer" might readily have possessed himself of the facts contained in, my last, and his imperti- nence in charging on Mr. Norman the responsibility. of hie rashness, ignorance and misapprehension is amusing to his opponents and pitiable to his frieneht. Your readers ere this have doubtlese discovered that bad Mr. Norman been more amenable Is tine private interests of "A Ratepayer," and consequently lee/ alive to the " pulalic weal," the warning voice had not :Ana beard, and if in the future it again breaks silence it may safely be regarded, loan artful decoy. The spectacle of " A Ratepayer," while convicted of publishing statements without stiatlaw of foundation, parad- ing his ability to hit bard, and big-willingness to hit true, is characteristic of the man and even, if after this exposé, his diatribes are continued I shall not be surprised, for Back wounding calumny The whitest virtue strikes. What king el strong Can tie the gall up in the slanderer's tongue? Faithfully yours, VERACITY.

WARRINGTON COUNCIL CHAMBER. , Sir,—lt seems to be the special aim of a few of our local parliaments to hold themselves up4o the ridicule of the rest of the nation. With one or two enceptional instance', our own Corporation has so far managed to keep out of the fierce light that beats upon publlc•bodies, as upon public individuals. Row long this will be-the case it is bard to say. My own opinion is that if thae teachings of Comaellor Mackie are to be adhered to, we shall not be very long before we may do away altogether with nouniciparelections and make arrangements with the, governors of lunatic asylums for a chelp and constant supply of town council- lors. When a town councillor rises in his place and states that "they were come not as partisans to gauge each other mentally, morally, or physicully, but politically," and of course implies that to their keenest and hardest wor!ting political adherents shall belong all the, honours of the Conn. cil Chamber, he preaches a doctrine that is simply suicidal to the best interests of the town. Why should Councillor Mackie deplore the election of-" two. able Liberals "simply because "it had done more to smash, not the Mandi, but the Conservative party of Warrington than all the other blunders which had boon committed ?" Think of this, townsmen ! the Consermtive party are smashed in conse- quence of the election of " two able Liberals." All I can say of this is, the Liberal party will run the risk of smashing if the Conservatives will kindly search out from their smashed body two able Conservatives ; but as they do not gauge them meatally, but only politically, I fear their task is hopeless. As Councillor Mackie standa pledged to "propose any other gentleman whom the party bad been pleased to select," we may look forward to Councillor Bolton being selected to fill the position of chief magistrate, on his way to donning the aldermanic gown. This is no unlikely prospect, as no one can doubt for a moment the political energy of that gentleman. But what of Councillor Mackie's prespects? Surely with all the didactic skill displayed before the minor lights of the Council Chamber there should be a fair chance in the running for him. Is it, that the political idol before which he has prostrated himself, is not a welcome guest in the councils of his party ? Councillor Mackie seems to think that to hold Conservative opinions is proof of a man's wisdom. I should rather say that to throw silk ha's up to the ceiling of the club-room on the receipt of a false telegram, or to take down a "picture" and smash it, simply because the original Proved himself, in wiatiorniabove and beyond his party, is a sign of mental abotration. Councillor Platt did well in repudiating the suggestion that "there Would be no attempt to wrest tial vacant Neat

div.p: from the Conservatives." Such pledges no gentleman should be entitled to give ; they remind us too much of hole and corner Work. ad.

But the climax of the meeting came In the severely aronitary speech of the new Alderman. In our Council Chamber we certainly want tone. This we cannot have, nnlesswe take a very much different coursein the future than we have in the past. Not that T for a moment accept the idea that .•the leading gentlemen of Warrington" mettle sole pos- sessors of that culture that alone gives tone and weight to the deliberation of a company of;men. It will rather be felt by those who feel the full weight of responsibility, and have at heart the well-being of their fellow townsmen. That the leading gentlemen of Warrington have not this feeling It, clear by their abdicating their duty as townsmen. On has to be carefel and keep off personalities, or it would be easy to give a reason for the " degeneration " deplored by Alder- man Crosfield. As a cure for this, I should advise the formation of a new party, "The People's Party," and let nrs push Liberals and Tories aside, and, instead of working far the social influence of the large manufacturers," let us work for the well-being of the people. CLIFFORD DIX. March 9th, 1885,

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Belgians are withdrawing from the stations estab- lished by them in Eastern Africa. Mr Chamberlain has written a letter to the Land Nation. Outten Society, la which he says he is not in favour of the 'nationailsation of the land. _

An outbreak of typhoid fever exists at Burnley. Daring the past few weeks no fewer than 21 cases have been re- ported to the authorities and five deaths have occurred. The Royal yacht Osborne is ordered to be out of the dockyard hands at Portsmouth on the 20th inst., in order that she may proceed to Holyhead and embark the Prince and Princess of Wales on the following Saturday. EXTENSIVE EMBEZZLEMENT.--- At Guisborough Police Court, on Friday, Edward Hampden Allbrook was charged with embezzling £4,000, the property of the Thatched House Club, London. The prisoner was handed over to the custody of Scotland-yard police officers. Form MEN DnowNED.—lt was reported from Silloth on Friday that the Caledonian, from Dublin, which has arrived there, and Kate (fishing lugger) were in collision that morning eight miles north of the Chickens, and the latter stink. Of the crew, four of the men were drowned and four saved.

EMIGIUTION ow Pwal CEILDREN.-At a meeting of ladies, held at Marlborough, on Friday, under :the presi- dency of Lady Frederick Bruce, it was decided to take all the pauper children from the Wiltshire workhouse and send them to Canada. A thousand girls will be first des- patched.
PUBLIC MOURNING FOR THE DEATH OF GENERAL GORDON.

A cordial response WAS given at Dover on Fridayeto the request of the Mayor that the inhabitants should observe the day as one of mourning for the loss of General Gordon. A special funeral service was held at the Parish Church, which was attended by the Mayor and Corporation and a large 1 congregation.—A. special service in commemoration of General Gordon and the officers and men fallen in the • Soudan, was held at St. Paul's Cathedral on Friday morn- ing. There was a very large congregation, during the assembling of which Chopin 's " Marche Funebre" was played on the organ. The opening sentences of the Burial Service were sung, and, after an anthem, the Bishop of New- castle delivered an address. The Archbishop of Canterbury was amongst those present.—The Commemoration Service I held at Chichester Cathedral on Friday morning was attended by a large congregation. The Bishop of Cinches- ; ter delivered an address, in which he observed that Gordon's I name would shine brighter for his devotion to a desperate canse.—A special service was held at one 'o'clock on Friday, inthe Manchester Cathedral. Au address was given by the Bishop, who paid a touching tribute to General Gordon, and those who had fallen in the war. . A service took place at Westminster Abbey, and was at. I tended by eriOrtngul congregation. which included r officers and non4Orittillegotted Officers of the liVal Engi- neers, to which General Gordon belongel.

ARREST OF FENIANS IN PARIS. The report of the arrest of the Fenian leaders in Paris is confirmed, and has caused an immense sensation. James Stephens, Morrisey, and Eugeae Davies will probably be expelled. Mrs. Stephens was also arrested, but was released. Warrants for the expulsion of several other Fenian leaders have been issued.
Paws, FRIDAY ArrsratoON.—The Fenian leaders, Ste- phens, Davis, and Leroy, together with two German Anarch- ists, have been conducted to the Belgium frontier.
THE AFGHAN -FHONTIaI, QUESTION:

The Press Association understands that Sir Peter Lnms- den has been instructed to coinmunisate to the Ameer of Afghanistan,. or to his chief representative at Herat, the sub- stance of the retreement as to the maintenance for the pre- sent of the military status quo, which has now been con- cluded between the British and Russian Governments. The announcement which the Prime Minister made upon the subject on Friday evening was received in the House of Commons with an almost general sense of relief as appar- ently affording an improved prospect in political circles. The opinion is freely expressed that the agreement with Russia announced by Mr. Gladstone is only intended as a temporary measure to avert the possibility of an immediate rupture. It is understood that Sir Peter Lumsden has been given very full discretionary powers In the event of collision between the Russian and Afghan outpost!. It is stated that the Russian claim to Penjdhe, based as it wan upon ethnographical even more than geographical grounds, has not been withdrawn, and there have been grave reasons tor believing that the Russian outposts were slowly and surely approaching the coveted position. On Friday morning, however, M. De Steal received a despatch from St Petersburg, the contents of which were so-important that he communicated at once with Lord Granville, and subse- quently called upon kis lordship.—During the afternoon I Lord Gratville communicated to his ccileagues the sub- stance of his conversation with the Russian ambassador, and subsequentlY an informal Cabinet Connell was held in Mr Gladstone's private room in the House of Commons, at which the form of the Premier's announcement to the House was den/tied upon. Undue value, the Central News states, should not be attached to the new agreement, as in consenting to suspend her military movements in the Afghan frontier regions Russia has plainly intimated that she abandons for the present, at any rate, none of the claims which she has recently put forward,moreparticularly In regard to Pen:ffitte, the acquisition of which ',absolutely necessary 'for the protection of her Turkorsan subjects. Lord Granville, so far, has declined to admit the validity of Russian arguments on this matter; but he hos accepted the principle that the present difficulties clearly demon- strate the necessityfor settling the Afghaa boundary ques- tion upon permanent basis. Meanwhile, Sir Peter Lumsdett retains the wide discretionary power conferred upon him some time since, and he will continuo to act as circumstances may render necessary.
THE REBELS AT SUAKIM. -OSMAN
DIGNA DEFIANT.

Canto, Faroa—v-flabors-.:—.A.- telegram; irOm Sir Gerald Graham to Sir Evelyn Barieg, this morning, stated that the rebels attacked the advanced British outposts on Thursday night. Several men were killed or wounded. The rebel loss is unknown. The audacity of the enemy's. around Suakim is increasing. Native spies report that Osman Digna's followers are in reckless spirits, and defiant. It is believed to be certain that the British troops will be strongly opposed, as the Arabs seem determined and anxious to fight. Osman has sent out orders for all the tribes supporting him to assemble at Tamanieb. A very large body of rebels and many pro- minent sheikhs have already arrived there. A large number of tribesmen are now reported to have firearms in place of emirs. It is possible they may have received them from Khartoum.

The Imperial Tube-Works, Wolverhampton, have received an order from the War Office for forty miles of wrought iron pipes for shipment to Suakim. Sudden orders were received at Chatham on Friday evening directing H.M.S. Leander to be got ready for sea by April 20th.

ENOLAND AND RESSNA, : STATEMENT OF Mn. GI4,P• STONE—Mr. GrAnsvosx,,replying to Mr. Richards as to 'settling the Afghan frontier dispute by correspondence, and for invoking aid of kiendly powers as regarded the dif- ference which existed. said the question divided itself into two subjects ;:one was the agreement made sometime ago be- tween England and Russia to ascertain what should be the frontier between Russia and Afghanistan, by " inquiry and correspolence," and the other if advances had been made by Russian andiAfghan forces on the•debatable ground. With regard to the second of these, it had been agreed that there should be no further advances to be made on either side. With regard to the first part of the question, that of ascertaining the frontier by raoeneol correspondeoce.

It would, therefore, be premature for him to at present pronounce as to the solution that might or might not be proper.—Sir S. NORTROOTE asked if the agreement was a permanent arrangement.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the agreement was not a formal instruction, but was an engage- ment entered iato by diplomatic correspondence and was to last as long as there was occasion for it. (Laughter.)— Sir.% CAMPBELL inquired whether the Government con- sidered .the Afghans had advanced from the boundary, and Whether that had not been an incentive to Russia to ad- ivanae.--TMr. W. E. FORSTER ' wished to know whether the agreement referred to by Mr. Gladstone was a new one.— Mr. Gtemosrown said he was not quite certain as to the pro- visions of the old agreement. The present was an agree- ment which had grown out of a recent diplomatic corres- pondence, and referred to the existing state of things. THE REDISTRIBUTION BILL—The House then went into Committee on the Redistribution Bill. On clause three, which disfranchised Macclesfield and Sandwich, on account of corrupt practices in 1880, Mr. SLAG° moved to omit Macclesfield from the operation of the clause, on the ground that its trade and population entitled it to Parliamentary representation.—The Arroromy.Gd7SEßAL pointed out that the clause did not extinguish Macclesfield, but joined it to Congleten for the purpose of voting for the county under the name of Macclesfield division. He pointed out that the corruption of Macclesfield in 1880 had been gross.—After some discussion Mr. Slagg withdrew his proposal, but said when they came to the schedule he should move the addi- tion of Oxford, Chester, and Gloucester to the boroughs to be disfranchised.—The amendment was negatived without a division.—Mr. Grmzs moved the omission of the clause.— A discussion ensued, and the clause was retained by 153 to 31 votes. On clause 4 being proposed, which enacted that the city of London should return two members and no more, Mr R N FOWLER moved the omission of the word.s from the clause which provided that two of the four mem- bers which at present represented tke city of London should be taken away. He said no case had been made out for taking away two members from the city.—Sir C DILKE opposed the proposal, and said if the city of London . was treated, on the population basis it ought only ice have one member. After con- aiderable discussion, there voted—For the amend- ment, 117. ; against, 182.—The clause was then agreed to, as were clausea 5, and 8. On clause 7, which relates to boroughs with ttoir boundaries altered. Mr. ARNOLD Moss- LET moved an amendment to prevent freeholders as suck in future votiog at elections in Eristol, Nottingham. Norwich, and Exeter.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL opposed the amend- ment, and It was withdrawn, and progress was reported.— The Hope adjourned at twenty-five minutes past one.
