Da. O'HARA Comm:a-man FOR TRIAL.—At the Prescot Police Court on Saturday, before Mr. W. L. Evans, Daniel Murray O'Hara, better known as "Doctor O'llara" who had Lean twice previously remaaded, was again brought-up on a,charge of feloniously using under a false ooloturi,the forms of the County Court of Lancashire, holden ataSt.' Helens. The prisoner was defended by Mr. Murphy, of Liverpool. From the evidence it appeared that in October hat a woman named Ellen Fairhurst consulted the Irrisoner and he charged her the sum of 5.3 ed for medicine- and ad- vice. She was unable to pay the money at the time, and went in service at Huyton.. The prisoner subsequently visi-, ted her and served upon her a paper which he asset ted was a summons front the County Court at St. Helensand added that unless she-paid the money at ones he wouli. send the bailiffs to her residence. There were also two other simi- lar charges against the prisoner. For the defence Mr. Murphy contended that a rebuke from the County Court Judge at S. Helens a month or two ago was a sofecient Dunishmeit upon the prisoner. The Bench decided to com- mit the prisoner for trial at the neat Liverpool Assisas.

TO THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH-WEST WARD. Leniss AND GENTLIMRN,—At the urgent request of a large number of Ratepayers I have consented to allow myself to be nominated for the vaeanay in the representation of this Ward in the Town Council, caused by the election of Councillor John Crtsfield as an Alderman of the Borough. As a native of Warrington, the good government of the Borough at large, is to me a matter of great importance, and having resided for many years in the South-West Ward, it is only natural that, If elected, I thou'd be especially desirous a promoting the interests of my neighbours and fellow-rate- 'payers. I think that the present depressed condition of trade calls for the practice t f the strictest possible economy consistent with prudence and efficiency In every deeartment of municipal work, and if you honour me with your confidence, I shall spare no effort to aid in suatt an administration of our Town's Affairs as will help to frustrate any unnecessary expenditure and will promote a permanent reduotion of the rates. Respectfully requesting your support, I beg to remain, ladles and gentlemen. Your obedient servant, CHARLES SAWKINS BURGESS. 31, Bold-street, Warrington, March sth, 1885. MUNICIPAL ELECTION, WARRINGTON. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE SOU ill-WEST WAR.). LIDIES AND GIENTLEMXN,—I have, at the request Of It large and n.fluential hody of Ratepayers, consented, to become a Candidate for the vacant seat in tbe Town Council. If elected, it will be my earoest endeav,ur to merit your confidence, by opposing extravagant expenditure and support- ing all measures which will be conducive to-the real interests ot the Borough an all oocasions. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen. Yours obediently. EROS. JOLLEY.

RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.— MANCHESTER SHIP OANAL.—At a duly convened meeting of the Unworn Improvement Commissioners, held in the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, Runcorn, on Thursday, the .sth day of February, it was unanimously rese'ved—ll That the Runcorn Improvement 0 trnmissloner. oppose, in Parliament, a private Bill, intltuled • A Bill to authorize the construction of a Ship Oanal to Manchester, and for other purposes,' and that the Parliamentary and Legal Committee, with Mr. W. H. ' Linaker, solicitor, be and are hereby empowered and instructed to take all neeetsary steps by petition to Pirliament, and other- wise.for giving effect to snob opposition, and for the protection of the rights and interests of the Board and of the district of Runcorn, in relation to the objects of such Bill. That the costs land expenses, whether already incurred or to be incurred, of and attendant upon the Commissioners' opposition to the said Bill, be charged upon the general district rate, or other the public funds or rates under the oontrol cf the said Commis- sioners. W. BROWEES, Secretary. Town Hall, Runcorn, March sth, 1885, PARLIAMENT.—BESSION 1885. THE MANCHE:STEM BRIE' CANAL. VW" HEREAS a MEETING of the OWNERS and I TV IIATEPAYE,tB of the Improvement Act District of ltuneorn. in the 0 runty of Cheshire, was held on Thursday, I the sth day of February, 1885, in ths Bethesda School-room, Vicar-street, Runcorn, in pursuance of the Act of the 35th and 36th Vie., cap. 91, intltuled "An At to authorize the ap- plication of Funds of Municipal Ocrporations and other govern- ' lug bodies in certain oases;" And Whereas at tee paid Meeting, held at the time and place afore.ald, I, as Chairman of such meeting, and in com- pliance with the statute. proroted the following resolution : •• That the consent of the Owners and Ratepayers of the Im- provement Act Distr et of Runcorn be. and the same is hereby, give to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners to oppose In Par lament a Private Bill now before Parliament, intituled, • A Bill to authorize the construction of a Ship Canal to Man- chester, and for other purposes,' and this meeting hereby ap- proves and eantlons the applying of the General District Rate. or other the Public Foods or Rates under the c-tnlirol of the said Improvement Commissioners, to the payment of the costs and expense* attending such °pp, sition ;'' And Whereas the said resolution on being put to the meet- ing was not carried, whereupon demand was made that such question should be decided by a Poll of the Owners and Rate- payers; And Whereas a Poll was accordingly taken in manner pro- vided by the Public Health Act, 1875, and the Schedules thereto. I hereby declare that at such Poll of the Owners and Rate- payers, the above resolution, was carried. Dated at Runcorn this 2nd day of March, 1885. ROBERT SHAW, Returning Officer._

PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED, HOLBORN BLISS, LONDON.—THIRTY-SIXTH AN- NUAL REPORT, for the year ending 3 tst DECEMHESt. 1884. The Directors have much pleasure in presenting their report and a counts for the year 1884. The funds have been increased during the vec.r by the sum of £362,606 • namely, in the Ordinary Branch £158,840, and in the Inlustrl'al Branch £702,766, raising the total assets of the Company to £4,711,464. ORDINARY BRANCH. The new business of this branch for the year consists of 11,823 Policies. ensuing the SUM of £1,359,341, and producing a New Annual Premium Income of £58,580. The Premiums of the year are £238,868, being an Increase of £15,881 over the year 1883. Toe total increase for the Rust three years of the Quinquenolum is £97,611. The claims of the year amount to £112,474. The num- ber of Deaths was 644, aud 45 Endowment Assurances ma- tured. The rate of expenditure of the Brancit slightly exceeds Ten per cent on the Premium Income. The number of Policia; in foree in this Branch is 61,835. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH. The Premiums received during the year are £2,644,516, being an iccrease of £140,206, The Claims of the year amount to £l.O 3,273. The number of Deaths was 121,658. The number of Policies in force in this Branch is 6,302,890. The total exper sea of the Branch show a reduction in the rate of expenditure of fully Two per cent on the Premium In- come. and theatre, in which latter place plays were acted and lectures and debates held. Thence they went to a spacious room in which a great public dance was held once a week, the remaining evenings being given up to military drill. He was told that every man was obliged to drill twice a week, and sometimes the men of five or six villages were brigaded together for more extended practise, and once a in the fortnight following harvest the men of a county as- sembled together for rifle shooting and ahem fights. In this wav there was maintained an army of six millions of soldiers ready at a moment's notice. The village co-opera- tive store having been inspected, he was informed that there were no public-howsee and if anyone wanted beer or spirits they drank them at their own homes. They next visited the cement works, one marked feature of them being the absence of long chimnies and smoke, and he was told that these works were carried on by the workmen themselves. At first this socialistic experiment involved frequent quar- rels amongst the workmen, but that soon came to an end. Every year they elected a strong governing committee, whose decisions they obeyed. The men divided all the profits, only paying a qait-rent to the State for the land on which the works stood. In every factory in England the working hours were limited to eight hours, and DO over- time was allowed. (Hear, hear.) As he stood the bell rang and the workmen Caine trooping past. They were not like those he remembered, tired, sullen, and downcast, trudging many of them to wretched homes two ranee away, but fresh, cheerful, unwearied, going to their pretty homes close at hand, with full capacity for gardening or for mental culture, ov for public amusement or domes- tic pleasure during the remaing part of the afternoon and evening. Everywhere the land was well tilled, every- where the houses were comfortable and of various degrees of beauty, and everywhere the men were educated, indepen- dent, and self-respecting. The lecturer then went on to say that having asked the parson how all this change was brought about, the latter told him that a hundred years ago in the closing decade of the 19th century, the rent of land in England had fallen nearly 70 per cent., 25,000,000 of acres were out of cultivation, tenant farmers were every- where ruined, and the towns were crowded.
